Heterogeneous Effects of Continuous Treatments via Conditional Modified Treatment PoliciesThanks: Corresponding Author: huling@umn.edu

Samhita Pal Affiliation: and    Department of Biostatistics Affiliation: Jared D. Huling    Vanderbilt University Medical Center Affiliation: Division of Biostatistics and Health Data Science, University of Minnesota
Abstract

For continuous treatments such as drug dose or ventilator intensity, a key clinically actionable question is whether a modest, patient-specific adjustment to the current dose would help or harm, rather than whether to treat at all. Standard estimands such as average or conditional dose-response functions require positivity across a wide range of doses, an assumption that routinely fails in observational clinical data where protocols tie dosing to patient characteristics. We develop a framework for characterizing heterogeneity in the effects of small shifts (“nudges”) of a continuous treatment. We study two estimands: the conditional nudge effect, the expected outcome change if an individual at dose aa with covariates 𝒙\bm{x} had their dose shifted by δ\delta, and the conditional modified treatment policy (CMTP) effect, which averages the nudge over the observed dose distribution given covariates. Both are identified under weak, shift-specific local positivity and exchangeability conditions. Recasting the δ\delta-shift as a two-arm comparison through a duplicated-data construction, we develop weighting and A-learning estimators based on squared-error and negative log-likelihood losses, introduce augmented versions that reduce variance without changing the target, and establish asymptotic normality of proposed estimators. Simulations support the theory, and an analysis of mechanical ventilation data from MIMIC-III identifies patient profiles predicted to benefit from a modest reduction in mechanical power.

Keywords: Causal inference; effect modification; stochastic interventions; positivity; treatment effect heterogeneity; observational data

1 Introduction

In many clinical and policy settings, the key questions are how much a specific amount of a continuous treatment, such as a drug dose or a ventilator setting, affects patient outcomes and whether the same amount benefits all patients equally, not just whether the treatment works at all. In patients with Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS), for example, the mechanical power (MP) of a ventilator has effects on mortality that vary along a continuum as it is changed. Further, the effect of MP on mortality is unlikely to be constant across patients. For example, a patient with severely reduced lung compliance or high vasopressor requirements may respond differently to the same ventilator settings compared with a patient with milder illness. Thus, the population-average dose-response function (ADRF) does not characterize key variation that clinicians need to make individualized decisions. Understanding which patients benefit from what degree of change to MP is thus helpful for making personalized treatment recommendations that improve outcomes without exposing low-risk patients to unnecessary ventilator changes.

Such continuous treatments introduce challenges for heterogeneous treatment effect estimation that go beyond those encountered with binary exposures. With a binary treatment, the positivity assumption requires only that every patient has a positive probability of receiving either treatment; with a continuous treatment, positivity requires that every patient has positive density at every dose level in the support, a condition that is often implausible when clinical protocols constrain treatment values based on patient characteristics. In ARDS patients, ventilation guidelines explicitly restrict MP settings based on measures of the patient’s condition. For example, the PaO2/FiO2 ratio, a pre-treatment covariate characterizing the degree of acute hypoxemia, induces strong confounding by determining both the severity of disease and the range of MP values clinicians will administer (Huling et al., 2024; Papazian et al., 2019). As a result, some combinations of disease severity and ventilator power are rarely or never observed in practice, and global positivity over the full treatment range fails. Heterogeneity exacerbates this problem, e.g., the same MP may be relatively safe in a compliant lung but concentrates tidal energy in a reduced volume of recruitable lung units in poorly compliant lungs, increasing the risk of ventilator-induced injury (Siegel et al., 2019).

Beyond average dose-response curves, individualized care benefits from an understanding of how dose-response relationships and marginal improvements from small shifts vary with patient characteristics 𝑿\bm{X} and current dose AA. To date, little work has been done at the intersection of heterogeneous treatment effect estimation and continuous treatments. Zhu et al. (2024) study heterogeneous effects of multivariate continuous treatments with high-dimensional covariates through a representation-learning approach. Recently, Shin et al. (2025) define estimands such as the contrast surface τa1,a0​(𝒙)=𝔼⁡{Y⁡(a1)−Y⁡(a0)∣𝑿=𝒙}\tau_{a_{1},a_{0}}(\bm{x})=\mathbb{E}\{Y(a_{1})-Y(a_{0})\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}\} and a multivariate treatment-effect variable-importance measure (MTE-VIM), where Y⁡(a)Y(a) is the potential outcome under treatment A=aA=a. However, these procedures require strong positivity over high-dimensional covariates and a wide treatment range, which is often implausible in realistic settings. Due to failure of positivity in continuous treatments, these contrast surfaces are simply not identified over the full treatment range.

In this article, we focus on a novel local-shift estimand designed to mitigate the positivity limitations discussed above. Specifically, we ask: for patients with covariates 𝑿=𝒙\bm{X}=\bm{x}, what is the expected change in outcome if treatment is shifted by a clinically modest increment δ\delta from the value actually received? Because this policy changes treatment only around its values realized in practice, it requires substantially weaker positivity than the full ADRF or global contrast surfaces in that identification needs positive density only near the observed treatment level. The analysis therefore remains anchored to routinely used, clinically feasible doses. Consequently, recommendations based on our local-shift estimands involve only modest departures from standard practice, potentially making uptake of recommendations more palatable for practitioners. Related work on incremental propensity-score interventions and other stochastic treatment distributions tied to the observed treatment process has developed causal effects that avoid global positivity, including recent nonparametric work on heterogeneous, positivity-robust contrasts (Wen et al., 2023; McClean et al., 2024); our methods instead focus on continuous-treatments and shift the observed dose by a fixed amount δ\delta. Our approach is also motivated by modified treatment policies for continuous exposures (Jiang and Huling, 2025; Díaz et al., 2023), which interpret treatment shifts as targeting a hypothetical post-modification population.

This work focuses on two novel estimands: the conditional nudge effect, which characterizes how an individual at dose aa with covariates 𝒙\bm{x} would change if nudged by δ\delta, and the conditional modified treatment policy (CMTP) effect, which averages the nudge effect over the observed treatment distribution given covariates. The resulting estimands support individualized recommendations of the form “for patients with profile 𝑿=𝒙\bm{X}=\bm{x}, a small decrease in MP is expected to improve outcome.” The CMTP is identified under a weak, local positivity condition, enabling its valid estimation in data where treatment values are driven by clinical protocols. To estimate the conditional nudge effect and CMTP, we use the connection between MTPs and binary treatments shown in Jiang et al. (2026) that uses a duplicated-data construction comparing AA with A+δA+\delta. With this reparameterization we develop loss function based estimators in both a weighting and A-learning setup, with both squared-error and negative-log-likelihood losses (Chen et al., 2017) for different outcome types. We introduce augmented versions that leave the target unchanged but reduce variance. We provide large-sample theory for the nudge estimators and obtain CMTP inference either by direct estimation or by plug-in from the estimated nudge surface.

A further practical advantage of our approach is that it does not require estimating the generalized propensity score (GPS), a conditional density that is notoriously difficult to model reliably with high-dimensional covariates and whose inverse can produce extreme, unstable weights (Naimi et al., 2014; Colangelo and Lee, 2026; Huling et al., 2024). Instead, the duplicated-data construction requires only a propensity model for the binary arm indicator Λ\Lambda, a standard binary regression problem that avoids the conditional density estimation the GPS requires. In contrast, most existing work on continuous treatments is built around the GPS r⁡(a,𝒙)=fA|𝑿​(a∣𝒙)r(a,\bm{x})=f_{A\mid\bm{X}}(a\mid\bm{x}), which plays the balancing role of the binary propensity score in identifying and estimating the average dose-response function μ⁡(a)=𝔼​{Y⁡(a)}\mu(a)=\mathbb{E}\{Y(a)\} under unconfoundedness and positivity (Robins et al., 2000; van der Laan and Robins, 2003; Díaz and van der Laan, 2013; Hirano and Imbens, 2004; Imai and van Dyk, 2004; Austin, 2018; Zhao et al., 2020), with subsequent contributions developing doubly robust nonparametric and weighting estimators (Kennedy et al., 2017; Ai et al., 2021). Remedies for GPS instability include direct inverse-GPS estimation (Colangelo and Lee, 2026), covariate balancing weights (Yiu and Su, 2018; Vegetabile et al., 2021; Fong et al., 2018), and kernel-based independence weights (Kallus and Santacatterina, 2019; Martinet, 2020; Huling et al., 2024), though none circumvent the more fundamental requirement that global positivity over the full treatment support must hold for the ADRF to be identified.

The remainder of this article is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the estimands and identification assumptions, formulates the nudge and CMTP effects through optimization problems, develops both averaged and direct CMTP estimators, extends the framework to exponential-family outcomes, and Section 3 defines the empirical estimators. Section 4 presents asymptotic normality results, Section 5 reports simulations, and Section 6 applies the method to MIMIC-III mechanical ventilation data. Finally, we present our concluding remarks in Section 7.

2 Methodology

Let (𝑿,A,Y)∼F𝑿,A,Y(\bm{X},A,Y)\sim F_{\bm{X},A,Y}, where 𝑿∈𝒳⊆ℝp\bm{X}\in\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{p} denotes pre-treatment covariates, A∈𝒜⊆ℝA\in\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathbb{R} a continuous treatment or dose, and Y∈𝒴⊆ℝY\in\mathcal{Y}\subseteq\mathbb{R} the outcome. We write fAf_{A} and f𝑿f_{\bm{X}} for the marginal densities of AA and 𝑿\bm{X}, fA|𝑿​(a∣𝒙)f_{A\mid\bm{X}}(a\mid\bm{x}) for the conditional density of AA given 𝑿\bm{X}, and f𝑿,A​(𝒙,a)f_{\bm{X},A}(\bm{x},a) for their joint density. The corresponding distribution functions are FA​(a)=ℙ⁡(A≤a)F_{A}(a)=\mathbb{P}(A\leq a), F𝑿​(𝒙)=ℙ⁡(𝑿≤𝒙)F_{\bm{X}}(\bm{x})=\mathbb{P}(\bm{X}\leq\bm{x}), FA|𝑿​(a∣𝒙)=ℙ⁡(A≤a∣𝑿=𝒙)F_{A\mid\bm{X}}(a\mid\bm{x})=\mathbb{P}(A\leq a\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}), and F𝑿,A​(𝒙,a)=ℙ⁡(𝑿≤𝒙,A≤a)F_{\bm{X},A}(\bm{x},a)=\mathbb{P}(\bm{X}\leq\bm{x},A\leq a). The observed data are nn i.i.d. copies {(𝑿i,Ai,Yi)}i=1n\{(\bm{X}_{i},A_{i},Y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}. We suppress subscripts on densities and distribution functions when no ambiguity arises.

2.1 Estimands

We work in the potential-outcomes framework where for each dose level a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}, Y⁡(a)Y(a) denotes the outcome that would be observed were the treatment set to aa. The causal conditional average dose-response function (CADRF), μ⁡(a,𝒙)≡𝔼⁡[Y⁡(a)∣𝑿=𝒙]​ for ​a∈𝒜,\mu(a,\bm{x})\equiv\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,Y(a)\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}\,\right]\text{ for }a\in\mathcal{A}, has been the main approach to characterizing heterogeneity of effect for continuous-valued treatments in the literature. The CADRF describes how the conditional mean potential outcome varies with aa given 𝑿=𝒙\bm{X}=\bm{x}. Estimating μ⁡(a,𝒙)\mu(a,\bm{x}) nonparametrically is challenging in practice because 𝑿\bm{X} may be high-dimensional and because identification requires (i) no unmeasured confounding Y⁡(a)⟂A|𝑿Y(a)\perp A\mid\bm{X} and (ii) local overlap/positivity, informally, that all doses aa of interest occur with nonzero probability at covariate value 𝒙\bm{x}. Motivated by these challenges and by policy questions about the effects of small changes to practice, instead of targeting the entire CADRF, we focus on two local shift estimands that are identified under assumptions of differing strength and offer distinct, but related, interpretations. We define the conditional nudge effect at dose aa and covariates 𝒙\bm{x}, which captures the expected change in outcome from nudging the dose aa at 𝒙\bm{x} by a small increment δ\delta (with a,a+δ∈𝒜a,a+\delta\in\mathcal{A}), as τδ​(a,𝒙)≡𝔼⁡[Y⁡(a+δ)−Y⁡(a)∣𝑿=𝒙].\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x})\;\equiv\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,Y(a+\delta)-Y(a)\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}\,\right]. Compared to the CADRF μ⁡(a,𝒙)\mu(a,\bm{x}), the local nudge surface τδ​(a,𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x}) is often a more tractable estimand. First, it typically has lower effective complexity because it is a local contrast, in which terms depending on 𝒙\bm{x} alone cancel in the outcome model. Second, identification only requires overlap locally between aa and a+δa+\delta rather than across the entire range of aa, a condition that is far more plausible when δ\delta is small. Third, we show that the contrast can be estimated directly, without specifying and fitting a full outcome regression model for μ⁡(a,𝒙)\mu(a,\bm{x}). Finally, our nudge estimators can admit doubly robust strategies so that consistency still holds if either of the two nuisance components (the arm propensity model or the outcome regression) is correctly specified.

The policy analog of the conditional nudge effect, the CMTP effect, averages that nudge over the natural (observed) distribution of treatment at 𝒙\bm{x}:

τδ​(𝒙)≡𝔼⁡[Y⁡(A+δ)−Y⁡(A)∣𝑿=𝒙]=𝔼⁡[τδ​(A,𝒙)∣𝑿=𝒙].\displaystyle\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x})\;\equiv\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,Y(A+\delta)-Y(A)\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}\,\right]\;=\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\tau_{\delta}(A,\bm{x})\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}\,\right]. (1)

Thus, CMTP is the conditional expectation of the nudge surface with respect to the conditional law of A|𝑿=𝒙A\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}, providing a covariate-specific measure of the consequence of uniformly shifting everyone’s dose by δ\delta in that stratum. The first expression in (1) is the definition; the second equality, which represents the CMTP as the average of the nudge surface, holds under the mean nudge exchangeability condition (Assumption 3(A) below) but is not needed for identification of τδ​(𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x}) itself. The CMTP effect τδ​(𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x}) enjoys several advantages over the conditional nudge surface. First, it is causally identifiable under weaker, shift-specific assumptions, making it more robust to confounding and positivity violations. Second, it can be obtained by marginalizing the estimated nudge over A|𝑿A\mid\bm{X}, even though its identification requires strictly weaker conditions than the nudge itself. Finally, because τδ​(𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x}) is a function of 𝒙\bm{x} alone, its modeling burden is lower: estimation involves either a direct one-step CMTP loss in 𝒙\bm{x} or a plug-in average over A|𝑿=𝒙A\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}. While marginal modified treatment policies allow for shifts that depend on AA and 𝑿\bm{X}, they still require the user to specify the form of the shift a priori; the CMTP more directly assesses effect heterogeneity in response to a shift and thus yields a clearer sense of which covariates may drive differential response.

2.2 Causal assumptions and identification

Having defined the conditional nudge and CMTP effects, we now state the causal assumptions under which they can be identified from the observed data.

Assumption 1 (Consistency).

For all (a,𝐱)(a,\bm{x}) with fA|𝐗​(a∣𝐱)>0{f_{A\mid\bm{X}}(a\mid\bm{x})}>0, if A=aA=a then Y=Y⁡(a)Y=Y(a).

Assumption 2 (Positivity).

The shifted dose is feasible: for all (a,𝐱)(a,\bm{x}), if fA|𝐗​(a∣𝐱)>0f_{A\mid\bm{X}}(a\mid\bm{x})>0 then fA|𝐗​(q⁡(a,𝐱)∣𝐱)>0f_{A\mid\bm{X}}\big(q(a,\bm{x})\mid\bm{x}\big)>0.

Assumption 3 (Exchangeability).

For all (a,𝐱)(a,\bm{x}) with fA|𝐗​(a∣𝐱)>0{f_{A\mid\bm{X}}(a\mid\bm{x})}>0 and q⁡(a,𝐱)q(a,\bm{x}) as the shift/policy map (e.g., q⁡(a,𝐱)=a+δq(a,\bm{x})=a+\delta), the following hold:

  1. (A)

    Mean nudge effect exchangeability:
    𝔼[Y(q(a,𝒙))−Y(a)|𝑿=𝒙,A=a]=𝔼[Y(q(a,𝒙))−Y(a)|𝑿=𝒙].\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,Y\!\big(q(a,\bm{x})\big)-Y(a)\,\middle|\,\bm{X}=\bm{x},\,A=a\right]=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,Y\!\big(q(a,\bm{x})\big)-Y(a)\,\middle|\,\bm{X}=\bm{x}\right].

  2. (A′)

    Conditional mean policy exchangeability:
    𝔼[Y(q(a,𝒙))|𝑿=𝒙,A=a]=𝔼[Y(q(a,𝒙))|𝑿=𝒙,A=q(a,𝒙)].\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,Y\!\big(q(a,\bm{x})\big)\,\middle|\,\bm{X}=\bm{x},\,A=a\right]=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,Y\!\big(q(a,\bm{x})\big)\,\middle|\,\bm{X}=\bm{x},\,A=q(a,\bm{x})\right].

Assumption 2 is substantially weaker than the positivity assumption required for estimating the causal average dose response function and can be made to hold by design, since q⁡(a,𝒙)q(a,\bm{x}) is a user-specified function. For the fixed shift q⁡(a,𝒙)=a+δq(a,\bm{x})=a+\delta the assumption cannot hold exactly at the boundary of a bounded dose support; throughout, we therefore restrict attention to the region {a:fA|𝑿​(a∣𝒙)>0​ and ​fA|𝑿​(a+δ∣𝒙)>0}\{a:f_{A\mid\bm{X}}(a\mid\bm{x})>0\text{ and }f_{A\mid\bm{X}}(a+\delta\mid\bm{x})>0\}, although a boundary-respecting shift in the spirit of Haneuse and Rotnitzky (2013) could be used instead. We note that Assumption 3 is substantially weaker than the mean exchangeability assumption required for estimating the causal average dose response function. The typical mean exchangeability assumption immediately implies Assumption 3 holds; further, if the conditional mean potential outcome function is smooth in aa, then this assumption becomes more plausible as q⁡(a,𝒙)q(a,\bm{x}) becomes closer to aa.

Proposition 1.

Under Assumptions 1, 2, and 3(A) and (A′), for every (a,𝐱)(a,\bm{x}) with fA|𝐗​(a∣𝐱)>0f_{A\mid\bm{X}}(a\mid\bm{x})>0, the conditional nudge effect is identified in terms of the observed data as 𝔼[Y|𝐗=𝐱,A=a+δ]−𝔼[Y|𝐗=𝐱,A=a]=τδ(a,𝐱)\mathbb{E}[Y|\bm{X}=\bm{x},A=a+\delta]-\mathbb{E}[Y|\bm{X}=\bm{x},A=a]=\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x}).

Proposition 2.

Let m0(a,𝐱):=𝔼[Y∣𝐗=𝐱,A=a]m_{0}(a,\bm{x}):=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x},A=a] denote the observed outcome regression. Under Assumptions 1, 2 and 3(A′), for f𝐗f_{\bm{X}}-almost every 𝐱\bm{x}, the CMTP effect is identified in terms of the observed data as 𝔼⁡[m0​(A+δ,𝐱)|𝐗=𝐱]−𝔼⁡[Y|𝐗=𝐱]=τδ​(𝐱)\mathbb{E}[{m_{0}}(A+\delta,\bm{x})|\bm{X}=\bm{x}]-\mathbb{E}\left[Y|\bm{X}=\bm{x}\right]=\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x}).

We emphasize that the identification formula in Proposition 2 involves the observed outcome regression m0​(a,𝒙)m_{0}(a,\bm{x}) rather than the counterfactual CADRF, which is not identified under our assumptions. Notably, the CMTP effect requires only condition (A′) while the nudge surface requires both (A) and (A′), making precise the sense in which the CMTP is identified under strictly weaker conditions. These propositions provide the identification results that justify our estimation procedures, which we develop in the remainder of this section. The first shows that the conditional nudge effect can be recovered from observed conditional mean differences, whereas the second establishes that the CMTP effect is identified by contrasting the average of the outcome regression evaluated at the shifted dose with the average observed outcome.

2.3 Approach 1: Estimating the CMTP via the conditional nudge

In this section, we introduce a data duplication technique (Díaz et al., 2023) that allows us to directly estimate both the conditional nudge effect and the CMTP without the need to model the entire outcome regression surface. We create a duplicated treatment AΛA_{\Lambda} that is, with marginal probability 1/21/2, either the observed dose AA or an inverse-shifted dose A−δA-\delta (the inverse of the policy shift we ultimately care about). This requires the shift map a↦q⁡(a,𝒙)a\mapsto q(a,\bm{x}) to be invertible (e.g., q⁡(a,𝒙)=a+δq(a,\bm{x})=a+\delta). We then define the arm label

Λ=12​if ​AΛ=A−δ⁡(shifted arm),Λ=−12​if ​AΛ=A⁡(original arm),\Lambda=\tfrac{1}{2}\ \text{if }A_{\Lambda}=A-\delta\ (\text{shifted arm}),\hskip 18.49988pt\Lambda=-\tfrac{1}{2}\ \text{if }A_{\Lambda}=A\ (\text{original arm}){,}

so that, conditional on (𝑿=𝒙,AΛ=a)(\bm{X}=\bm{x},A_{\Lambda}=a), the event Λ=1/2\Lambda=1/2 corresponds to units whose original dose was a+δa+\delta, while Λ=−1/2\Lambda=-1/2 corresponds to units with original dose aa. Let πΛ​(𝒙,a):=ℙ⁡(Λ=12∣𝑿=𝒙,AΛ=a)\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a):=\mathbb{P}\big(\Lambda=\tfrac{1}{2}\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x},A_{\Lambda}=a\big) denote the conditional probability that an observation in the duplicated data belongs to the shifted arm, given covariates and the duplicated treatment value. Then, a direct calculation using ℙ(Λ=1/2)=ℙ(Λ=−1/2)=1/2\,\mathbb{P}(\Lambda=1/2)=\mathbb{P}(\Lambda=-1/2)=1/2\, gives πΛ​(𝒙,a)=gA|𝑿​(a+δ∣𝒙)/{gA|𝑿​(a+δ∣𝒙)+gA|𝑿​(a∣𝒙)},\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a)={g_{A\mid\bm{X}}(a+\delta\mid\bm{x})}/\big\{{g_{A\mid\bm{X}}(a+\delta\mid\bm{x})+g_{A\mid\bm{X}}(a\mid\bm{x})}\big\}, where gA|𝑿g_{A\mid\bm{X}} is the conditional density (or mass) of AA given 𝑿\bm{X}.

2.3.1 Weighting estimator for the nudge effect

We target τδ​(a,𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x}) by minimizing a balanced squared-loss on the duplicated sample. For any candidate contrast f⁡(a,𝒙)f(a,\bm{x}) define the conditional population risk

ℓW(f;a,𝒙)=𝔼[w(a,𝒙,Λ){Y−Λf(a,𝒙)}2|𝑿=𝒙,AΛ=a],\ell_{W}(f;a,\bm{x})=\mathbb{E}\!\left[w(a,\bm{x},\Lambda)\,\big\{Y-\Lambda\,f(a,\bm{x})\big\}^{2}\;\middle|\;\bm{X}=\bm{x},\ A_{\Lambda}=a\right], (2)

where expectations are with respect to the joint law of (Y,AΛ,𝑿,Λ)(Y,A_{\Lambda},\bm{X},\Lambda). Identification requires only that the weights satisfy the arm-balancing condition

w⁡(a,𝒙,12)​ℙ​(Λ=12∣𝑿=𝒙,AΛ=a)=w⁡(a,𝒙,−12)​ℙ​(Λ=−12∣𝑿=𝒙,AΛ=a),w(a,\bm{x},\tfrac{1}{2})\,\mathbb{P}\!\left(\Lambda=\tfrac{1}{2}\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x},A_{\Lambda}=a\right)=w(a,\bm{x},-\tfrac{1}{2})\,\mathbb{P}\!\left(\Lambda=-\tfrac{1}{2}\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x},A_{\Lambda}=a\right), (3)

in which case, for strictly positive weights, the unique minimizer is f∗​(a,𝒙)=τδ​(a,𝒙)f^{*}(a,\bm{x})=\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x}) as shown later in Proposition 3. Several convenient choices satisfy (3). First, IPW: w⁡(a,𝒙,1/2)=πΛ​(𝒙,a)−1,w(a,\bm{x},1/2)=\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a)^{-1}, and w(a,𝒙,−1/2)={1−πΛ(𝒙,a)}−1\ w(a,\bm{x},-1/2)=\{1-\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a)\}^{-1}. Second, Density-ratio: either w(a,𝒙,1/2)={1−πΛ(𝒙,a)}/πΛ(𝒙,a),w(a,𝒙,−1/2)=1w(a,\bm{x},1/2)=\{1-\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a)\}/\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a),\ w(a,\bm{x},-1/2)=1, or the symmetric alternative with the roles reversed. These can be computed directly from gA|𝑿g_{A\mid\bm{X}} using (1−πΛ​(𝒙,a))/πΛ​(𝒙,a)=gA|𝑿​(a∣𝒙)/gA|𝑿​(a+δ∣𝒙).({1-\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a)})/{\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a)}={g_{A\mid\bm{X}}(a\mid\bm{x})}/{g_{A\mid\bm{X}}(a+\delta\mid\bm{x})}. Third, Overlap: w⁡(a,𝒙,12)=1−πΛ​(𝒙,a),w⁡(a,𝒙,−12)=πΛ​(𝒙,a)w(a,\bm{x},\tfrac{1}{2})=1-\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a),\ \ w(a,\bm{x},-\tfrac{1}{2})=\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a). A advantage of the IPW and overlap weights is that they require modeling only a conditional probability rather than a conditional density, which is often substantially more challenging to estimate reliably (Huling et al., 2024). To reduce variance without changing the target, we use an augmented version that subtracts any function m⁡(a,𝒙)m(a,\bm{x}) of (AΛ,𝑿)(A_{\Lambda},\bm{X}):

ℓW,aug(f;a,𝒙)=𝔼[w(a,𝒙,Λ){Y−m(a,𝒙)−Λf(a,𝒙)}2|𝑿=𝒙,AΛ=a].\ell_{W,\mathrm{aug}}(f;a,\bm{x})=\mathbb{E}\!\left[w(a,\bm{x},\Lambda)\,\big\{Y-m(a,\bm{x})-\Lambda\,f(a,\bm{x})\big\}^{2}\;\middle|\;\bm{X}=\bm{x},\ A_{\Lambda}=a\right]. (4)

The conditional losses above characterize the pointwise population target at a fixed value of (AΛ,𝑿)=(a,𝒙)(A_{\Lambda},\bm{X})=(a,\bm{x}); the empirical estimator minimizes the corresponding marginal risk ℓW,aug​(f):=𝔼⁡[ℓW,aug​(f,AΛ,𝑿)]\ell_{W,\mathrm{aug}}(f):=\mathbb{E}[\ell_{W,\mathrm{aug}}(f;A_{\Lambda},\bm{X})] (and analogously ℓW​(f)\ell_{W}(f)) over a working class f⁡(a,𝒙)=𝜽⊤​𝒃​(a,𝒙)f(a,\bm{x})=\bm{\theta}^{\top}\bm{b}(a,\bm{x}), made precise in Section 3, and thus estimates the projection of the pointwise nudge contrast onto the basis class. This direct weighted-learning formulation is motivated by the contrast-learning/subgroup-identification framework of Chen et al. (2017). The following proposition formalizes the key identification step behind our weighting approach. Under the duplicated-arm construction (AΛ,Λ)(A_{\Lambda},\Lambda) and any choice of weights w⁡(a,𝒙,Λ)w(a,\bm{x},\Lambda) that satisfy the arm-balancing condition (3), minimizing the conditional squared loss (2) (equivalently, its marginal average ℓW​(f)\ell_{W}(f)) recovers the unique contrast that equates the two arm-specific conditional means at (𝒙,a)(\bm{x},a). Consequently, the population minimizer is the conditional nudge effect τδ​(a,𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x}).

Proposition 3.

Suppose the weights are strictly positive and satisfy (3), and that fA|𝐗​(a∣𝐱)>0f_{A\mid\bm{X}}(a\mid\bm{x})>0, so that 0<πΛ​(𝐱,a)<10<\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a)<1 by Assumption 2. Then the minimizers fW∗f_{W}^{*} of ℓW​(f)\ell_{W}(f) and fW,aug∗f_{W,\mathrm{aug}}^{*} of ℓW,aug​(f)\ell_{W,\mathrm{aug}}(f) over measurable functions are almost everywhere unique and satisfy fW∗(a,𝐱)=fW,aug∗(a,𝐱)=𝔼[Y|𝐗=𝐱,A=a+δ]−𝔼[Y|𝐗=𝐱,A=a],f^{*}_{W}(a,\bm{x})=f_{W,{\mathrm{aug}}}^{*}(a,\bm{x})=\mathbb{E}[Y|\bm{X}=\bm{x},A=a+\delta]-\mathbb{E}[Y|\bm{X}=\bm{x},A=a]{,} which equals τδ​(a,𝐱)\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x}) under the conditions of Proposition 1.

Proposition 3 demonstrates that the conditional loss identifies the pointwise nudge effect. When the loss is averaged over the marginal distribution of (AΛ,𝑿)(A_{\Lambda},\bm{X}) and minimized over a finite-dimensional working model, the resulting estimator targets the corresponding projection of this pointwise effect. Moreover, the augmentation function m⁡(a,𝒙)m(a,\bm{x}) is included for precision rather than identification. As mm depends only on (AΛ,𝑿)(A_{\Lambda},\bm{X}), it is subtracted equally from the two duplicated arms at a fixed value of (AΛ,𝑿)(A_{\Lambda},\bm{X}); since the balancing condition (3) implies 𝔼[w(a,𝒙,Λ)Λ∣𝑿=𝒙,AΛ=a]=0\mathbb{E}[w(a,\bm{x},\Lambda)\Lambda\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x},A_{\Lambda}=a]=0, the subtraction does not alter the population contrast identified by the loss. A natural choice is a working outcome regression, m(a,𝒙)≈𝔼[Y∣A=a,𝑿=𝒙],m(a,\bm{x})\approx\mathbb{E}[Y\mid A=a,\bm{X}=\bm{x}], or equivalently in the duplicated-arm notation, m(a,𝒙)≈𝔼[Y∣AΛ=a,𝑿=𝒙].m(a,\bm{x})\approx\mathbb{E}[Y\mid A_{\Lambda}=a,\bm{X}=\bm{x}]. This removes outcome variation explained by the treatment level and covariates before estimating the nudge/CMTP contrast, and can therefore improve efficiency. In applications, mm may be estimated using a parametric regression, splines, or flexible machine-learning methods. Correct specification of mm is not needed for identification of the nudge/CMTP effects; rather, the quality of mm affects the variance of the resulting estimator. The additional first-order variability due to estimating mm is incorporated in the augmented A-learning asymptotic result in Section 4.

2.3.2 A-learning estimator for the nudge effect

An alternative to the weighting construction, in the spirit of A-learning, removes main-effect variation by centering the arm indicator rather than by reweighting the loss. To this end, we define the recoded arm indicator Λ~:=Λ+12∈{0,1}\widetilde{\Lambda}:=\Lambda+\tfrac{1}{2}\in\{0,1\} and let

ℓA(f;a,𝒙)=𝔼[{Y−(Λ~−πΛ(𝒙,a))f(a,𝒙)}2|𝑿=𝒙,AΛ=a].\displaystyle\ell_{A}(f;a,\bm{x})=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\big\{Y-(\widetilde{\Lambda}-\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a))\,f(a,\bm{x})\big\}^{2}\;\middle|\;\bm{X}=\bm{x},\ A_{\Lambda}=a\right]. (5)

Minimizing ℓA\ell_{A} over ff yields the same target f∗​(a,𝒙)=τδ​(a,𝒙)f^{*}(a,\bm{x})=\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x}) (the centering removes main-effect contamination). This is formalized in Proposition 4. As with weighting, we introduce an augmented A-learning loss

ℓA,aug(f;a,𝒙)=𝔼[{Y−m(a,𝒙)−(Λ~−πΛ(𝒙,a))f(a,𝒙)}2|𝑿=𝒙,AΛ=a],\displaystyle\ell_{A,\mathrm{aug}}(f;a,\bm{x})=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\big\{Y-m(a,\bm{x})-(\widetilde{\Lambda}-\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a))\,f(a,\bm{x})\big\}^{2}\;\middle|\;\bm{X}=\bm{x},\ A_{\Lambda}=a\right], (6)

which preserves the target but improves efficiency by removing prognostic variation through m⁡(a,𝒙)m(a,\bm{x}). The corresponding marginal losses are ℓA​(f):=𝔼⁡[ℓA​(f,AΛ,𝑿)]\ell_{A}(f):=\mathbb{E}[\ell_{A}(f;A_{\Lambda},\bm{X})] and ℓA,aug​(f):=𝔼⁡[ℓA,aug​(f,AΛ,𝑿)]\ell_{A,\mathrm{aug}}(f):=\mathbb{E}[\ell_{A,\mathrm{aug}}(f;A_{\Lambda},\bm{X})]. As in Proposition 3, the A-learning objective regresses the outcome on the centered treatment indicator Λ~−πΛ​(𝒙,a)\widetilde{\Lambda}-\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a), interacted with a basis in (a,𝒙)(a,\bm{x}), and identifies the same contrast. Centering removes main-effect variation, so the population first-order condition isolates the difference between the two treatment levels at (a,𝒙)(a,\bm{x}) so that the minimizer of ℓA​(f)\ell_{A}(f) is τδ​(a,𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x}). Subtracting any outcome regression m⁡(a,𝒙)m(a,\bm{x}) in the augmented loss ℓA,aug​(f)\ell_{A,\mathrm{aug}}(f) has no effect on bias, as augmentation only partials out outcome variation as a function of covariates and thus reduces variance without affecting identification.

Proposition 4.

Suppose fA|𝐗​(a∣𝐱)>0f_{A\mid\bm{X}}(a\mid\bm{x})>0, so that 0<πΛ​(𝐱,a)<10<\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a)<1 by Assumption 2. Then the minimizers fA∗f_{A}^{*} of ℓA​(f)\ell_{A}(f) and fA,aug∗f_{A,\mathrm{aug}}^{*} of ℓA,aug​(f)\ell_{A,\mathrm{aug}}(f) over measurable functions are almost everywhere unique and satisfy fA∗(a,𝐱)=fA,aug∗(a,𝐱)=𝔼[Y|𝐗=𝐱,A=a+δ]−𝔼[Y|𝐗=𝐱,A=a],f^{*}_{A}(a,\bm{x})=f^{*}_{A,{\mathrm{aug}}}(a,\bm{x})=\mathbb{E}[Y|\bm{X}=\bm{x},A=a+\delta]-\mathbb{E}[Y|\bm{X}=\bm{x},A=a]{,} which equals τδ​(a,𝐱)\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x}) under the conditions of Proposition 1.

Overall, this duplicated-arm formulation is simple to implement, accommodates a wide choice of balancing weights, and supports variance-reducing augmentation, while directly targeting the localized causal contrast τδ​(a,𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x}) that underpins the CMTP via τδ​(𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x}).

2.3.3 CMTP estimation by averaging over the conditional nudge

Both the weighting and A-learning estimators target the local contrast, that is, the conditional nudge effect τδ​(a,𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x}) at dose aa and covariates 𝒙\bm{x} under a shift of size δ\delta. The CMTP at covariate level 𝒙\bm{x} averages this effect over the conditional distribution of the observed dose given 𝑿=𝒙\bm{X}=\bm{x}. If gA|𝑿​(a∣𝒙)g_{A\mid\bm{X}}(a\mid\bm{x}) denotes the corresponding conditional density or mass function, then τδ​(𝒙)=𝔼⁡[Y⁡(A+δ)−Y⁡(A)∣𝑿=𝒙]=∫τδ​(a,𝒙)​gA|𝑿​(a∣𝒙)​𝑑a,\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x})=\mathbb{E}\!\left[Y(A+\delta)-Y(A)\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}\right]=\int\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x})\,g_{A\mid\bm{X}}(a\mid\bm{x})\,\mathrm{d}a, with the integral replaced by a sum for discrete AA. Thus, once τδ​(a,𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x}) is identified and estimated, the CMTP follows by averaging the conditional nudge over the exposure distribution at 𝒙\bm{x}. In practice, we represent the conditional nudge parametrically, for example f⁡(a,𝒙)=𝜽⊤​𝒃​(a,𝒙)f(a,\bm{x})=\bm{\theta}^{\top}\bm{b}(a,\bm{x}), and obtain a plug-in CMTP by projecting the fitted values f^​(Ai,𝑿i)\hat{f}(A_{i},\bm{X}_{i}) onto a lower-dimensional basis c⁡(𝒙)c(\bm{x}), writing τδ​(𝒙)≈𝜷⊤​c​(𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x})\approx\bm{\beta}^{\top}c(\bm{x}); the details are given in Section 3. While this plug-in approach is straightforward, it requires an initial fit of the entire nudge surface; in the next subsection we develop estimators that target the CMTP directly.

2.4 Approach 2: Direct estimation of the CMTP

Here, we propose a direct estimation method for the CMTP that does not require first estimating the local nudge effect τδ​(a,𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x}) and then averaging over the conditional distribution of A|𝑿=𝒙A\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}. Instead, the method uses the duplicated-arm construction to form an A-learning loss whose contrast depends only on 𝒙\bm{x}, so that the resulting estimator targets τδ​(𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x}) directly. A disadvantage of obtaining the CMTP from an initial nudge fit is the need to model the conditional nudge effect itself, a statistical task of higher complexity than modeling the CMTP alone. The construction exploits only Assumption 3(A′), mirroring the weaker identification requirements of the CMTP established in Proposition 2.

We work with a squared-error A-learning loss for directly estimating the CMTP in the main text and defer a weighting counterpart to Supplement A.1. The direct A-learning loss is similar to (5), except that we no longer model a local contrast at a fixed dose aa, and instead let the contrast depend only on the covariates 𝒙\bm{x}, integrating over the mixture distribution of AΛA_{\Lambda} given 𝑿=𝒙\bm{X}=\bm{x}. Concretely, recall that (5) targets the local nudge τδ​(a,𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x}). For the CMTP, we instead consider functions f:𝒳→ℝf:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} and define the direct A-learning CMTP loss ℓACMTP​(f,𝑿)=𝔼⁡[{Y−g⁡(𝑿,AΛ)​f​(𝑿)}2|𝑿],\ell_{A}^{\mathrm{CMTP}}(f;\bm{X})=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\big\{Y-g(\bm{X},A_{\Lambda})\,f(\bm{X})\big\}^{2}\;\middle|\;{\bm{X}}\right], where g⁡(𝑿,AΛ):=Λ~−πΛ​(𝑿,AΛ)g(\bm{X},A_{\Lambda}):=\widetilde{\Lambda}-\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{X},A_{\Lambda}) has conditional mean zero given (𝑿,AΛ)(\bm{X},A_{\Lambda}). The corresponding marginal loss is simply ℓACMTP​(f)=𝔼⁡[ℓACMTP​(f,𝑿)].\ell_{A}^{\mathrm{CMTP}}(f)=\mathbb{E}[\ell_{A}^{\mathrm{CMTP}}(f;\bm{X})]. This construction preserves the same centering idea as in (5), but now targets the aggregate effect τδ​(𝒙)=𝔼⁡{Y⁡(A+δ)−Y⁡(A)∣𝑿=𝒙}\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x})=\mathbb{E}\{Y(A+\delta)-Y(A)\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}\} rather than the local contrast at a fixed aa. We define h⁡(𝒙,a):=πΛ​(𝒙,a)​{1−πΛ​(𝒙,a)},h(\bm{x},a):=\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a)\big\{1-\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a)\big\}, so that g⁡(𝒙,AΛ)g(\bm{x},A_{\Lambda}) has conditional mean zero and conditional variance h⁡(𝒙,AΛ)h(\bm{x},A_{\Lambda}) given (𝑿,AΛ)(\bm{X},A_{\Lambda}). Under this unstabilized direct CMTP loss for measurable f:𝒳→ℝf:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}, the first-order condition (FOC) is 𝔼⁡[g⁡(𝑿,AΛ)​{Y−g⁡(𝑿,AΛ)​f​(𝑿)}|𝑿]=0,\mathbb{E}\Big[g(\bm{X},A_{\Lambda})\,\big\{Y-g(\bm{X},A_{\Lambda})f(\bm{X})\big\}\,\Big|\,{\bm{X}}\Big]=0, which yields the pointwise minimizer f∗​(𝒙)=𝔼⁡[g⁡(𝒙,AΛ)​Y∣𝑿=𝒙]/𝔼⁡[g2​(𝒙,AΛ)∣𝑿=𝒙]≡N⁡(𝒙)/D⁡(𝒙)f^{*}(\bm{x})={\mathbb{E}\big[g(\bm{x},A_{\Lambda})Y\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}\big]}/{\mathbb{E}\big[g^{2}(\bm{x},A_{\Lambda})\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}\big]}\equiv{N(\bm{x})}/{D(\bm{x})}.

Lemma 1.

Let m0​(a,𝐱)m_{0}(a,\bm{x}) be the outcome regression in Proposition 2. For every 𝐱\bm{x}, N⁡(𝐱)=𝔼⁡[h⁡(𝐱,AΛ)​{m0​(AΛ+δ,𝐱)−m0​(AΛ,𝐱)}∣𝐗=𝐱]N(\bm{x})=\mathbb{E}\big[h(\bm{x},A_{\Lambda})\,\{{m_{0}}(A_{\Lambda}+\delta,\bm{x})-{m_{0}}(A_{\Lambda},\bm{x})\}\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}\big], and D⁡(𝐱)=𝔼⁡[h⁡(𝐱,AΛ)∣𝐗=𝐱].D(\bm{x})=\mathbb{E}\big[h(\bm{x},A_{\Lambda})\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}\big].

Proof.

See the first part of the proof of Proposition 5 in the Supplementary Material∎

From Lemma 1, we see that the basic direct A-learning loss recovers a weighted CMTP, with weights h⁡(𝒙,AΛ)h(\bm{x},A_{\Lambda}), rather than the unweighted CMTP τδ​(𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x}). It is important to recognize that the expectations in Lemma 1 are taken with respect to the duplicated-arm mixture law of AΛA_{\Lambda} given 𝑿=𝒙\bm{X}=\bm{x}, whose conditional density is fAΛ|𝑿​(a∣𝒙)=12​{gA|𝑿​(a∣𝒙)+gA|𝑿​(a+δ∣𝒙)}f_{A_{\Lambda}\mid\bm{X}}(a\mid\bm{x})=\tfrac{1}{2}\{g_{A\mid\bm{X}}(a\mid\bm{x})+g_{A\mid\bm{X}}(a+\delta\mid\bm{x})\}, whereas the CMTP averages over the natural law of AA given 𝑿=𝒙\bm{X}=\bm{x}. Expressed against the natural law (the measure defining the CMTP), the implicit weight is πΛ​(𝒙,a)\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a). To eliminate the weighting entirely and directly target τδ​(𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x}), we therefore stabilize the conditional loss by dividing by πΛ​(𝑿,AΛ)\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{X},A_{\Lambda}):

ℓACMTP​(f,𝑿)=𝔼⁡[{Y−g⁡(𝑿,AΛ)​f​(𝑿)}2πΛ​(𝑿,AΛ)|𝑿],\displaystyle\ell_{A}^{\mathrm{CMTP}}(f;\bm{X})=\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\frac{\big\{Y-g(\bm{X},A_{\Lambda})\,f(\bm{X})\big\}^{2}}{{\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{X},A_{\Lambda})}}\,\Bigg|\,\bm{X}\Bigg], (7)

and, analogously, define the augmented version

ℓA,augCMTP​(f,𝑿)=𝔼⁡[{Y−m⁡(AΛ,𝑿)−g⁡(𝑿,AΛ)​f​(𝑿)}2πΛ​(𝑿,AΛ)|𝑿],\displaystyle\ell_{A,\mathrm{aug}}^{\mathrm{CMTP}}(f;\bm{X})=\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\frac{\big\{Y-m(A_{\Lambda},\bm{X})-g(\bm{X},A_{\Lambda})\,f(\bm{X})\big\}^{2}}{{\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{X},A_{\Lambda})}}\,\Bigg|\,\bm{X}\Bigg], (8)

for an arbitrary outcome regression m⁡(AΛ,𝑿)m(A_{\Lambda},\bm{X}). The following result shows that both stabilized losses identify the CMTP τδ​(𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x}), and that augmentation by m⁡(AΛ,𝑿)m(A_{\Lambda},\bm{X}) does not change the target. In particular, the unique pointwise minimizers of both stabilized A-learning CMTP losses recover the CMTP τδ​(𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x}). Because the marginal risk is the expectation of the conditional risk over 𝑿\bm{X}, namely ℓ⁡(f)=𝔼​{ℓ⁡(f,𝑿)}\ell(f)=\mathbb{E}\{\ell(f;\bm{X})\}, any measurable function that minimizes the conditional loss pointwise also minimizes the marginal loss; conversely, any marginal minimizer agrees with the pointwise minimizer almost surely.

Proposition 5.

Suppose Assumptions 1, 2, and 3(A′) hold. Under the stabilized direct A-learning CMTP loss (7) and its augmented counterpart (8) for an arbitrary function m⁡(AΛ,𝐗)m(A_{\Lambda},\bm{X}), let fA∗f_{A}^{*} and fA,aug∗f_{A,\mathrm{aug}}^{*} denote any minimizers of ℓACMTP​(f)\ell_{A}^{\mathrm{CMTP}}(f) and ℓA,augCMTP​(f)\ell_{A,\mathrm{aug}}^{\mathrm{CMTP}}(f), respectively. Then fA∗​(𝐱)=fA,aug∗​(𝐱)=𝔼⁡[m0​(A+δ,𝐱)−m0​(A,𝐱)∣𝐗=𝐱]=τδ​(𝐱),f_{A}^{*}(\bm{x})=f_{A,\mathrm{aug}}^{*}(\bm{x})={\mathbb{E}\big[m_{0}(A+\delta,\bm{x})-m_{0}(A,\bm{x})\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}\big]=\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x}),} where the expectation is over the natural conditional law of AA given 𝐗=𝐱\bm{X}=\bm{x} and the final equality follows from Proposition 2.

Proposition 5 shows that stabilizing the direct A-learning loss by πΛ\pi_{\Lambda} removes the implicit mixture-law weighting from Lemma 1, so that the resulting population minimizer targets the unweighted CMTP itself, with or without outcome-regression augmentation. At the population level, if f∗​(𝒙)=𝜷⊤​c​(𝒙)f^{*}(\bm{x})=\bm{\beta}^{\top}c(\bm{x}), the stabilized direct A-learning coefficient targets the unweighted L2​(P𝑿)L_{2}(P_{\bm{X}}) projection of the CMTP onto the span of cc: 𝜷Adir,0=arg⁡min𝜷⁡E⁡[{τδ​(𝑿)−𝜷⊤​𝒄​(𝑿)}2],\bm{\beta}^{\mathrm{dir},0}_{A}=\arg\min_{\bm{\beta}}E\left[\{\tau_{\delta}(\bm{X})-\bm{\beta}^{\top}\bm{c}(\bm{X})\}^{2}\right], since the stabilized score has constant conditional second moment, 𝔼⁡[g2​(𝑿,AΛ)/πΛ​(𝑿,AΛ)∣𝑿]=1/2\mathbb{E}[g^{2}(\bm{X},A_{\Lambda})/\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{X},A_{\Lambda})\mid\bm{X}]=1/2. If the working model is correctly specified, so that τδ​(𝒙)=𝜷0⊤​c​(𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x})=\bm{\beta}_{0}^{\top}c(\bm{x}), then 𝜷Adir,0=𝜷0\bm{\beta}^{\mathrm{dir},0}_{A}=\bm{\beta}_{0}. Our development thus far has relied on squared-error losses. The duplicated-arm construction extends naturally to canonical exponential-family losses for binary and other non-continuous outcomes. We next develop the link-scale A-learning nudge loss and its identification result, and use the resulting logistic-loss estimators in Sections 5 and 6.

2.5 Exponential family setup and logistic example

We extend the duplicated-arm construction and the weighting/A-learning losses to canonical exponential-family models, focusing on logistic loss for binary outcomes. Throughout this subsection we employ the working model in which, conditional on (A,𝑿)(A,\bm{X}), the outcome YY follows a one-parameter exponential family with natural parameter η{\eta} and negative log-likelihood (NLL) M⁡(y,η)=−y​η+b⁡(η),M(y,{\eta})=-y\,{\eta}+b({\eta}), so that μ(a,𝒙):=𝔼[Y∣A=a,𝑿=𝒙],η=k{μ(a,𝒙)},b′(η)=μ(η),\mu(a,\bm{x}):=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid A=a,\bm{X}=\bm{x}],\;{\eta}={k}\{\mu(a,\bm{x})\},\;b^{\prime}({\eta})=\mu({\eta}), where k{k} is the canonical link and μ⁡(η)\mu({\eta}) denotes the mean as a function of the natural parameter. Note that in this subsection μ⁡(a,𝒙)\mu(a,\bm{x}) denotes the observed outcome regression, written m0​(a,𝒙)m_{0}(a,\bm{x}) elsewhere in the paper, rather than the counterfactual CADRF of Section 2.1; the two coincide under the conditions of Proposition 1. In the logistic example with Y∈{0,1}Y\in\{0,1\}, we have η=log⁡(μ/(1−μ)),{\eta}=\log\left({\mu}/({1-\mu})\right), b⁡(η)=log⁡{1+exp⁡(η)},b({\eta})=\log\{1+\exp({\eta})\}, μ⁡(η)=eη/(1+eη).\mu({\eta})={e^{\eta}}/({1+e^{\eta}}). Here k{k} is the logit link and μ⁡(⋅)\mu(\cdot) is the expit function. In what follows we work directly with the NLL MM instead of squared loss, and interpret the resulting targets on the link scale, mapping back to the mean scale via μ⁡(⋅)\mu(\cdot) when needed. In this setting the mean-scale nudge effect at a given dose-covariate pair (a,𝒙)(a,\bm{x}) remains τδ​(a,𝒙)=μ⁡(a+δ,𝒙)−μ⁡(a,𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x})=\mu(a+\delta,\bm{x})-\mu(a,\bm{x}) under the conditions of Proposition 1, so that, under a canonical link, the nudge is fully determined by the change in the natural parameter η{\eta} induced by shifting the dose from aa to a+δa+\delta. For example, in the logistic case this evaluates to τδ​(a,𝒙)=μ⁡(η⁡(a+δ,𝒙))−μ⁡(η⁡(a,𝒙))=expit⁡(η⁡(a+δ,𝒙))−expit⁡(η⁡(a,𝒙)), where ​expit⁡(u)≡eu/1+eu,\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x})=\mu\bigl(\eta(a+\delta,\bm{x})\bigr)-\mu\bigl(\eta(a,\bm{x})\bigr)=\operatorname{expit}\!\bigl(\eta(a+\delta,\bm{x})\bigr)-\operatorname{expit}\!\bigl(\eta(a,\bm{x})\bigr),\text{ where }\operatorname{expit}(u)\equiv{e^{u}}/{1+e^{u}}, a nonlinear function of both aa and 𝒙\bm{x}, even when the working model for η⁡(a,𝒙){\eta}(a,\bm{x}) is linear in (a,𝒙)(a,\bm{x}). In parallel, the mean-scale CMTP at covariate level 𝒙\bm{x} satisfies, by Proposition 2, τδ​(𝒙)=𝔼⁡[μ⁡(A+δ,𝒙)−μ⁡(A,𝒙)∣𝑿=𝒙],\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x})=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mu(A+\delta,\bm{x})-\mu(A,{\bm{x}})\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}\bigr], so that τδ​(𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x}) aggregates the local nudge effects τδ​(a,𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x}) over the conditional distribution of A|𝑿=𝒙A\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}. In the logistic example this yields τδ​(𝒙)=𝔼⁡[expit⁡(η⁡(A+δ,𝒙))−expit⁡(η⁡(A,𝒙))∣𝑿=𝒙]\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x})=\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{expit}\!\bigl(\eta(A+\delta,\bm{x})\bigr)-\operatorname{expit}\!\bigl(\eta(A,\bm{x})\bigr)\,\mid\,\bm{X}=\bm{x}]. Here, we construct an A-learning analog based on the NLL, and defer the weighting version to the Supplementary Section A.2. Recall the recoded arm indicator Λ~:=Λ+12∈{0,1}\widetilde{\Lambda}:=\Lambda+\tfrac{1}{2}\in\{0,1\} and the arm propensity πΛ​(𝒙,a):=ℙ⁡(Λ~=1∣𝑿=𝒙,AΛ=a).\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a):=\mathbb{P}\bigl(\widetilde{\Lambda}=1\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x},A_{\Lambda}=a\bigr). For a candidate link-scale contrast f⁡(a,𝒙)f(a,\bm{x}), we define the A-learning NLL loss

ℓANLL(f;a,𝒙)=𝔼[−Y(Λ~−πΛ(𝒙,a))f(a,𝒙)+b((Λ~−πΛ(𝒙,a))f(a,𝒙))|𝑿=𝒙,AΛ=a],\ell_{A}^{\mathrm{NLL}}(f;a,\bm{x})=\mathbb{E}\Big[-Y\bigl(\widetilde{\Lambda}-\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a)\bigr)\,f(a,\bm{x})+b\bigl((\widetilde{\Lambda}-\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a))\,f(a,\bm{x})\bigr)\,\Big|\,\bm{X}=\bm{x},\ A_{\Lambda}=a\Big], (9)

where bb is the log-partition function. This loss regresses YY on the centered arm indicator Λ~−πΛ​(𝒙,a)\widetilde{\Lambda}-\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a) scaled by f⁡(a,𝒙)f(a,\bm{x}), mimicking the usual A-learning construction in a generalized-linear setting. The FOC with respect to ff leads to a contrast equation analogous to Supplementary equation (S3). Now, defining ℓANLL​(f)\ell_{A}^{\mathrm{NLL}}(f) as the marginal loss 𝔼⁡[ℓANLL​(f,AΛ,𝑿)]\mathbb{E}[\ell_{A}^{\mathrm{NLL}}(f;A_{\Lambda},\bm{X})], we state the following proposition.

Proposition 6.

Suppose the conditions of Proposition 1 hold and fA|𝐗​(a∣𝐱)>0f_{A\mid\bm{X}}(a\mid\bm{x})>0, so that πΛ​(𝐱,a)∈(0,1)\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a)\in(0,1). Assume ℓANLL​(f)\ell_{A}^{\mathrm{NLL}}(f), the marginal loss corresponding to (9), admits a unique minimizer fA∗​(a,𝐱)f_{A}^{*}(a,\bm{x}). Then fA∗​(a,𝐱)f_{A}^{*}(a,\bm{x}) satisfies μ⁡((1−πΛ​(𝐱,a))​fA∗​(a,𝐱))−μ⁡(−πΛ​(𝐱,a)​fA∗​(a,𝐱))=τδ​(a,𝐱).\mu\bigl((1-\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a))f_{A}^{*}(a,\bm{x})\bigr)-\mu\bigl(-\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a)\,f_{A}^{*}(a,\bm{x})\bigr)=\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x}).

In particular, in the logistic case this identity again links the minimizer fA∗​(a,𝒙)f_{A}^{*}(a,\bm{x}) to the arm-specific difference in success probabilities at (𝒙,a)(\bm{x},a), now expressed through the centered arm indicator Λ~−πΛ​(𝒙,a)\widetilde{\Lambda}-\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a). As in the squared-loss A-learning construction, the centering removes main-effect variation and isolates the arm contrast at (a,𝒙)(a,\bm{x}) on the link scale. As before, one may subtract an offset m⁡(a,𝒙)m(a,\bm{x}) from YY inside the linear term in (9) to reduce variance without affecting the population target. In the simulations presented in the Supplement, we focus on the non-augmented form for simplicity. Moreover, a discussion of a direct NLL loss for CMTP estimation can be found in Supplementary Section A.3.

3 Empirical estimators

The preceding population losses define weighting and A-learning through conditional risks under the duplicated-arm construction. In finite samples, we restrict τδ​(a,𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x}) to a semiparametric class and estimate it by minimizing empirical analogs of these losses. We next give the corresponding objectives, show that linear-basis representations yield (possibly weighted) least-squares estimators, and characterize their population limits. These empirical losses are optimized in our implementation and form the basis for the large-sample results and simulation studies in Sections 4 and 5. For compactness, we write 𝒁iλ:=(Ai−λ​δ,𝑿i),𝒃iλ:=𝒃⁡(𝒁iλ)​ and ​Yiλ:=Yi​ for ​λ∈{0,1}.\bm{Z}_{i}^{\lambda}:=(A_{i}-\lambda\delta,\bm{X}_{i}),\bm{b}_{i}^{\lambda}:=\bm{b}(\bm{Z}_{i}^{\lambda})\text{ and }Y_{i}^{\lambda}:=Y_{i}\text{ for }\lambda\in\{0,1\}. Thus 𝒁i0=(Ai,𝑿i)\bm{Z}_{i}^{0}=(A_{i},\bm{X}_{i}) denotes the observed arm and 𝒁i1=(Ai−δ,𝑿i)\bm{Z}_{i}^{1}=(A_{i}-\delta,\bm{X}_{i}) denotes the shifted arm. Define the duplicated empirical average ℙnΛ​fiλ:=n−1​∑i=1n∑λ=01fiλ.\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\Lambda}f_{i}^{\lambda}:=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{\lambda=0}^{1}f_{i}^{\lambda}. For A-learning, define the transformed basis 𝒃~iλ:={Λ~iλ−π^Λ​(𝒁iλ)}​𝒃iλ,\widetilde{\bm{b}}_{i}^{\lambda}:=\left\{\widetilde{\Lambda}_{i}^{\lambda}-\widehat{\pi}_{\Lambda}({\bm{Z}}_{i}^{\lambda})\right\}{\bm{b}}_{i}^{\lambda}, where Λ~iλ=λ\widetilde{\Lambda}_{i}^{\lambda}=\lambda is the arm indicator of the duplicated row and π^Λ​(𝒁iλ)=π^Λ​(Ai−λ​δ,𝑿i)\widehat{\pi}_{\Lambda}(\bm{Z}_{i}^{\lambda})=\widehat{\pi}_{\Lambda}(A_{i}-\lambda\delta,\bm{X}_{i}) is the estimated arm propensity evaluated at the row’s dose value. Then the A-learning empirical loss is

𝜽^A=arg​min𝜽⁡ℙnΛ​{Yi−𝜽⊤​𝒃~iλ}2={ℙnΛ​𝒃~iλ​𝒃~iλ⊤}−1​{ℙnΛ​𝒃~iλ​Yi}.\widehat{\bm{\theta}}_{A}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\bm{\theta}}\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\Lambda}\left\{Y_{i}-{\bm{\theta}}^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{b}}_{i}^{\lambda}\right\}^{2}=\left\{\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\Lambda}\widetilde{\bm{b}}_{i}^{\lambda}\widetilde{\bm{b}}_{i}^{\lambda\top}\right\}^{-1}\left\{\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\Lambda}\widetilde{\bm{b}}_{i}^{\lambda}Y_{i}\right\}.
Lemma 2 (Population limits of linear-basis nudge estimators).

Let τδ​(a,𝐱)\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x}) denote the conditional nudge effect and suppose we approximate it in a linear basis, τδ​(a,𝐱)≈𝛉⊤​𝐛​(a,𝐱),\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x})\approx\bm{\theta}^{\top}\bm{b}(a,\bm{x}), where 𝐛⁡(a,𝐱)∈ℝp\bm{b}(a,\bm{x})\in\mathbb{R}^{p} is a fixed vector of basis functions and 𝛉∈ℝp\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} is unknown. Suppose π^Λ\widehat{\pi}_{\Lambda} is uniformly consistent for πΛ\pi_{\Lambda}, the matrix 𝔼Λ​[hA​(AΛ,𝐗)​𝐛​(AΛ,𝐗)​𝐛​(AΛ,𝐗)⊤]\mathbb{E}^{\Lambda}[h_{A}(A_{\Lambda},\bm{X})\bm{b}(A_{\Lambda},\bm{X})\bm{b}(A_{\Lambda},\bm{X})^{\top}] is nonsingular, and the relevant second moments are finite. Then 𝛉^A→𝛉A∗\widehat{\bm{\theta}}_{A}\to\bm{\theta}_{A}^{*} in probability, where 𝛉A∗=arg​min𝛉∈ℝp𝔼[hA(AΛ,𝐗){τδ(AΛ,𝐗)−𝛉⊤𝐛(AΛ,𝐗)}2]Λ,\bm{\theta}_{A}^{*}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}}\mathbb{E}{{}^{\Lambda}}\left[h_{A}({A_{\Lambda}},\bm{X})\left\{\tau_{\delta}({A_{\Lambda}},\bm{X})-\bm{\theta}^{\top}\bm{b}({A_{\Lambda}},\bm{X})\right\}^{2}\right], with hA​(a,𝐱):=πΛ​(a,𝐱)​{1−πΛ​(a,𝐱)},h_{A}(a,\bm{x}):=\pi_{\Lambda}(a,\bm{x})\{1-\pi_{\Lambda}(a,\bm{x})\}{,} where 𝔼Λ\mathbb{E}^{\Lambda} denotes expectation under the duplicated-arm law of (AΛ,𝐗)(A_{\Lambda},\bm{X}), whose conditional density given 𝐗=𝐱\bm{X}=\bm{x} is the mixture 12​{gA|𝐗​(a∣𝐱)+gA|𝐗​(a+δ∣𝐱)}\tfrac{1}{2}\{g_{A\mid\bm{X}}(a\mid\bm{x})+g_{A\mid\bm{X}}(a+\delta\mid\bm{x})\}; each observation contributes to the projection through both of its duplicated rows.

In other words, under correct specification the A-learning estimator recovers the conditional nudge effect, while under misspecification it converges to the best hAh_{A}-weighted approximation of τδ​(a,𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x}) in the span of the basis. Because hA=πΛ​(1−πΛ)h_{A}=\pi_{\Lambda}(1-\pi_{\Lambda}), the projection emphasizes regions where the two duplicated arms overlap most, precisely where the nudge contrast is best identified. A similar result for the weighting loss is presented in Section A.4 of the Supplementary Material. For the direct CMTP estimators, we model the policy effect directly as τδ​(𝒙)≈f𝜷​(𝒙)=𝜷⊤​𝒄​(𝒙),\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x})\approx f_{\bm{\beta}}(\bm{x})={\bm{\beta}}^{\top}\bm{c}(\bm{x}), where 𝒄⁡(𝒙)\bm{c}(\bm{x}) is a lower-dimensional basis in 𝒙\bm{x}. The stabilized direct A-learning CMTP estimator is

𝜷^Adir=arg⁡min𝜷​ℙnΛ​{Yi−g^iλ​𝜷⊤​ci}2π^iλ=[ℙnΛ​(g^iλ)2π^iλ​ci​ci⊤]−1​[ℙnΛ​g^iλπ^iλ​ci​Yi].\hat{\bm{\beta}}^{\mathrm{dir}}_{A}=\arg\min_{\bm{\beta}}\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\Lambda}\frac{\{Y_{i}-\hat{g}_{i}^{\lambda}\bm{\beta}^{\top}c_{i}\}^{2}}{{\hat{\pi}_{i}^{\lambda}}}=\left[\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\Lambda}\frac{(\hat{g}_{i}^{\lambda})^{2}}{{\hat{\pi}_{i}^{\lambda}}}c_{i}c_{i}^{\top}\right]^{-1}\left[\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\Lambda}\frac{\hat{g}_{i}^{\lambda}}{{\hat{\pi}_{i}^{\lambda}}}c_{i}Y_{i}\right].

With augmentation by an outcome regression m^​(Ai−λ​δ,𝑿i)\hat{m}(A_{i}-\lambda\delta,\bm{X}_{i}),

𝜷^A,augdir=[ℙnΛ​(g^iλ)2π^iλ​ci​ci⊤]−1​[ℙnΛ​g^iλπ^iλ​ci​{Yi−m^​(Ai−λ​δ,𝑿i)}].\hat{\bm{\beta}}^{\mathrm{dir}}_{A,\mathrm{aug}}=\left[\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\Lambda}\frac{(\hat{g}_{i}^{\lambda})^{2}}{{\hat{\pi}_{i}^{\lambda}}}c_{i}c_{i}^{\top}\right]^{-1}\left[\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\Lambda}\frac{\hat{g}_{i}^{\lambda}}{{\hat{\pi}_{i}^{\lambda}}}c_{i}\{Y_{i}-\hat{m}(A_{i}-\lambda\delta,\bm{X}_{i})\}\right].

The estimators developed in this section provide the practical implementation of the weighting and A-learning procedures introduced in Section 2. By restricting the conditional nudge effect and the direct CMTP effect to finite-dimensional working models, the corresponding empirical objectives can be formulated as standard (weighted) least-squares problems, making estimation computationally straightforward. Lemma 2 further demonstrates that, under model misspecification, these estimators will converge to weighted L2L_{2} projections of the underlying causal effects onto the chosen basis rather than the true effects themselves, a standard property for semiparametric working models. These empirical estimating equations form the foundation for our inferential results. In the next section, we establish the large-sample behavior of our proposed estimators and derive asymptotic normality while accounting for the estimation of nuisance functions such as the duplicated-arm propensity model and, for the augmented estimators, the outcome regression model.

Conditions (C1)-(C3) are standard regularity assumptions that account for the estimation of the propensity component πΛ​(a,𝒙)\pi_{\Lambda}(a,\bm{x}): (C1) requires 𝜼^n\widehat{\bm{\eta}}_{n} to be asymptotically linear, so that the first-order effect of estimating 𝜼∗\bm{\eta}^{*} is captured by the influence function −J𝜼−1​U𝜼​(𝑶i,𝜼∗){-J_{\bm{\eta}}^{-1}U_{\bm{\eta}}(\bm{O}_{i};\bm{\eta}^{*})}, while (C2) and (C3) provide the empirical process (Donsker) control and smoothness needed for uniform Taylor expansion arguments in a neighborhood of 𝜼∗\bm{\eta}^{*}. Conditions (C4)-(C6) play the analogous role for the augmentation model m⁡(a,𝒙,𝝂)m(a,\bm{x};\bm{\nu}), which is an arbitrary working outcome regression and need not be correctly specified as 𝔼[Y∣A=a,𝑿=𝒙]\mathbb{E}[Y\mid A=a,\bm{X}=\bm{x}]. Together, these assumptions yield an asymptotically linear representation consisting of the main A-learning estimating function plus correction terms for nuisance estimation. Theorem 1 establishes that both A-learning nudge estimators are root-nn consistent and asymptotically normal, so that Wald-type inference can proceed from plug-in estimates of 𝑫\bm{D} and 𝚺A\bm{\Sigma}_{A} or 𝚺A,aug\bm{\Sigma}_{A,\mathrm{aug}}. Its second part indicates that, when the augmentation function is correctly specified and the stated orthogonality condition holds, augmentation can only reduce the asymptotic variance, supporting its routine use. A remark in the Supplementary Material records the usual projection simplification of the sandwich variance when 𝜼^n\widehat{\bm{\eta}}_{n} is an efficient estimator of 𝜼∗\bm{\eta}^{*} (Pierce, 1982), for both the unaugmented and augmented estimators. The nudge asymptotics also yield inference for the plug-in CMTP estimator obtained by averaging the fitted nudge over the conditional dose distribution; the formal statement, whose guarantees depend on how well that distribution can be estimated, is given as Corollary S1 in the Supplementary Material together with a remark on the same-sample projection implementation used in our numerical work. We therefore focus here on the direct CMTP estimator, which requires no such auxiliary estimate.

Unlike the plug-in approach above, the direct CMTP estimator of Section 3 targets the projection of τδ​(𝑿)\tau_{\delta}(\bm{X}) directly through a stabilized A-learning score, avoiding the intermediate estimation of the full conditional nudge surface τδ​(a,𝑿)\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{X}). Theorem 2 (Asymptotic normality of augmented direct CMTP A-learning).

Assume conditions (C1)-(C6), that 𝔼​{b⁡(𝐗)​b​(𝐗)⊤}\mathbb{E}\{b(\bm{X})b(\bm{X})^{\top}\} is nonsingular, that 𝔼​‖b⁡(𝐗)‖2<∞\mathbb{E}\|b(\bm{X})\|^{2}<\infty and 𝔼⁡(Y2)<∞\mathbb{E}(Y^{2})<\infty, and that πΛ​(a,𝐱,𝛈)≥c0>0\pi_{\Lambda}(a,\bm{x};\bm{\eta})\geq c_{0}>0 for all (a,𝐱)(a,\bm{x}) and all 𝛈\bm{\eta} in a neighborhood of 𝛈∗\bm{\eta}^{*}. If, in addition, 𝛈^n\widehat{\bm{\eta}}_{n} is an efficient estimator of 𝛈∗\bm{\eta}^{*}, then ΣC,aug=Σ~C,aug−BC,𝛈​V𝛈​BC,𝛈⊤\Sigma_{C,\mathrm{aug}}=\widetilde{\Sigma}_{C,\mathrm{aug}}-B_{C,\bm{\eta}}V_{\bm{\eta}}B_{C,\bm{\eta}}^{\top}, where Σ~C,aug=𝔼⁡{ψC,aug​(𝐎i,𝛉C∗,𝛈∗,𝛎∗)⊗2}\widetilde{\Sigma}_{C,\mathrm{aug}}=\mathbb{E}\{\psi_{C,\mathrm{aug}}(\bm{O}_{i};\bm{\theta}_{C}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*},\bm{\nu}^{*})^{\otimes 2}\}.

Theorem 2 demonstrates that the direct CMTP estimator is root-nn consistent and asymptotically normal for the L2​(P𝑿)L_{2}(P_{\bm{X}}) projection of the CMTP effect, with a sandwich variance accounting for the estimated propensity model. Because BC,𝝂=𝟎B_{C,\bm{\nu}}=\bm{0}, the outcome-regression augmentation contributes no first-order correction, so valid inference requires only a well-behaved propensity model while the working outcome model can be chosen freely to improve precision.

Finally, the same M-estimation strategy yields an asymptotic normality result for the logistic direct CMTP estimator, which uses the πΛ\pi_{\Lambda}-stabilized A-learning score with the logistic mean function and targets the direct CMTP projection on the link scale. The estimating function, the regularity conditions, and the formal statement are presented in Supplementary Theorem S2 in the Supplementary Material, together with its proof.

Together, these results establish asymptotically valid inference for the nudge and CMTP estimators under squared and logistic losses, while also showing that appropriate outcome-regression augmentation can improve efficiency without altering the target estimand. In Section 5 we examine how well these large-sample guarantees describe finite-sample behavior across a range of designs. A parallel asymptotic normality result for the logistic A-learning nudge estimator, which underpins the logistic nudge and average-CMTP analyses of Supplementary Section B.1 and Section 6, is stated and proved as Theorem S1 in the Supplementary Material.

5 Simulation Experiments

We evaluate finite-sample performance under a linear data-generating mechanism, where effects are defined on the mean scale; the experiment assesses bias under correct specification, compares the weighting schemes, and quantifies the precision gains from augmentation. We consider a continuous treatment AA and a low-dimensional covariate vector 𝑿=(X1,X2)⊤\bm{X}=(X_{1},X_{2})^{\top}. We generate the covariates i.i.d. with X1∼Unif⁡(−1,1)X_{1}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(-1,1) and X2∼Bernoulli⁡(0.7)X_{2}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(0.7). Conditional on 𝑿\bm{X}, the continuous dose AA follows an exponential distribution with mean exp⁡{2+0.5​X1+X2}\exp\{2+0.5X_{1}+X_{2}\} (equivalently, rate 1/exp⁡{2+0.5​X1+X2}1/\exp\{2+0.5X_{1}+X_{2}\}). Outcomes are drawn as Y|(A,𝑿)∼𝒩⁡{μ⁡(A,𝑿),1}Y\mid(A,\bm{X})\sim\mathcal{N}\{\mu(A,\bm{X}),1\} with μ⁡(A,𝑿)= 1+X1+X2+βA​A+α​A2+X1​{βA​X​A+β​A2},\mu(A,\bm{X})\;=\;1+X_{1}+X_{2}+\beta_{A}A+\alpha A^{2}+X_{1}\{\beta_{AX}A+\beta A^{2}\}, where we fix (α,β,βA​X,βA)=(−0.15, 0.2, 0.25,−0.5)(\alpha,\beta,\beta_{AX},\beta_{A})=(-0.15,\,0.2,\,0.25,\,-0.5) and take a shift size δ=0.5\delta=0.5. This specification induces a nonlinear and covariate-modulated relationship between the treatment and the outcome, while retaining a simple closed-form expression for the true causal effects under a shift intervention. Under the outcome model, our first causal target is the nudge effect, which is given by: τδ​(a,𝒙)=μ⁡(a+δ,𝒙)−μ⁡(a,𝒙)=βA​δ+2​α​a​δ+α​δ2+x1​(βA​X​δ+2​β​a​δ+β​δ2).\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x})=\mu(a+\delta,\bm{x})-\mu(a,\bm{x})=\beta_{A}\delta+2\alpha a\delta+\alpha\delta^{2}+x_{1}\bigl(\beta_{AX}\delta+2\beta a\delta+\beta\delta^{2}\bigr). This is a quadratic function of aa with coefficients depending on x1x_{1}. Also, using 𝔼⁡[A∣𝑿=𝒙]=exp⁡(2+0.5​x1+x2)\mathbb{E}[A\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}]=\exp(2+0.5x_{1}+x_{2}), we obtain an explicit expression for our second causal target, the CMTP effect τδ​(𝒙)=𝔼⁡{μ⁡(A+δ,𝒙)−μ⁡(A,𝒙)∣𝑿=𝒙}\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x})=\mathbb{E}\{\mu(A+\delta,\bm{x})-\mu(A,{\bm{x}})\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}\}, which averages the conditional nudge effect over the distribution of the observed treatment given covariates and in becomes βA​δ+α​δ2+2​α​δ​𝔼​[A∣𝑿=𝒙]+x1​(βA​X​δ+β​δ2+2​β​δ​𝔼​[A∣𝑿=𝒙]).\beta_{A}\delta+\alpha\delta^{2}+2\alpha\delta\,\mathbb{E}[A\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}]+x_{1}\bigl(\beta_{AX}\delta+\beta\delta^{2}+2\beta\delta\,\mathbb{E}[A\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}]\bigr). This serves as the ground truth when evaluating CMTP estimators. To evaluate estimators we project each target onto low-dimensional working bases. For the nudge effect we use the linear span of {1,A,X1,X2,A:X1,A:X2}\{1,\ A,\ X_{1},\ X_{2},\ A\!:\!X_{1},\ A\!:\!X_{2}\}; the corresponding population coefficients have closed forms (Intercept,A,X1,X2,A:X1,A:X2)=(βAδ+αδ2, 2αδ,βA​Xδ+βδ2, 0, 2βδ, 0).(\text{Intercept},A,X_{1},X_{2},A\!:\!X_{1},A\!:\!X_{2})=(\beta_{A}\delta+\alpha\delta^{2},\ 2\alpha\delta,\ \beta_{AX}\delta+\beta\delta^{2},\ 0,\ 2\beta\delta,\ 0). Similarly, for the CMTP effect we project onto {1,X1,X2}\{1,X_{1},X_{2}\}. Here, the true function τδ​(𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x}) is nonlinear in 𝒙\bm{x} through 𝔼⁡[A∣𝑿=𝒙]=exp⁡(2+0.5​x1+x2)\mathbb{E}[A\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}]=\exp(2+0.5x_{1}+x_{2}). Therefore, when we fit a linear working model in the basis c⁡(𝒙)=(1,x1,x2)⊤c(\bm{x})=(1,x_{1},x_{2})^{\top}, the target coefficient is the population least-squares projection 𝜷CMTP∗=arg⁡min𝜷∈ℝ3⁡𝔼⁡[{τδ​(𝑿)−𝜷⊤​𝒄​(𝑿)}2]={𝔼⁡[𝒄⁡(𝑿)​𝒄​(𝑿)⊤]}−1​𝔼​[𝒄⁡(𝑿)​τδ​(𝑿)].{\bm{\beta}}_{\mathrm{CMTP}}^{*}=\arg\min_{{\bm{\beta}}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\{\tau_{\delta}(\bm{X})-{\bm{\beta}}^{\top}\bm{c}(\bm{X})\right\}^{2}\right]=\left\{\mathbb{E}[\bm{c}(\bm{X})\bm{c}(\bm{X})^{\top}]\right\}^{-1}\mathbb{E}[\bm{c}(\bm{X})\tau_{\delta}(\bm{X})]. This projected coefficient vector serves as the ground truth for evaluating the CMTP coefficient estimators. We compare three base methods (Density, Overlap, A-learning) and their augmented versions under squared-error loss, all with a common linear working model; for the CMTP we consider both the average and direct constructions, giving twelve CMTP estimators. For each n∈{500,1000,5000}n\in\{500,1000,5000\} we generate independent datasets, fit all estimators, and record empirical root mean squared error (RMSE) for each coefficient, measuring how well they recover the true linear projections of τδ​(a,𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x}) and τδ​(𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x}).

Figure 1 reports coefficient-wise log-RMSE for n∈{500,1000,5000}n\in{\{}500,1000,5000{\}}, for the nudge coefficients. RMSE decreases with nn throughout; Density Ratio performs best at n=500n=500, whereas Overlap and A-learning decline more steeply and outperform it by n=5000n=5000. The nearly identical Overlap and A-learning curves agree with the theoretical expectation that, under correct nuisance specification, both target the same population projection. Augmentation lowers RMSE across the board. In the CMTP results shown in Table 1, we display coefficient-level bias, RMSE, and 95% Wald coverage for the A-learning, Density Ratio, and Overlap estimators under the squared error loss with and without augmentation. The three weighting approaches are nearly very similar in performance, with Overlap and A-learning typically matching or slightly outperforming Density Ratio; augmentation improves precision consistently, and direct CMTP estimation is competitive with, and at larger sample sizes occasionally more accurate than, averaging the estimated nudge, particularly with Overlap weighting. Coverage is close to nominal throughout, though the augmented intercept dips to roughly 0.92 at n=5,000n=5,000. Corresponding results for a logistic-outcome design are reported in Section B of the Supplement.

6 Analysis of Mechanical Power Data

We analyze data from a cohort of ICU patients who received invasive mechanical ventilation for at least 48 hours, originally assembled and studied by Serpa Neto et al. (2018). The dataset was extracted from the mimic-iii clinical database. For each patient, we define the continuous treatment AA as the mean of the minimum and maximum MP of ventilation (in Joules per minute) during the second 24-hour period in the ICU, and restrict attention to patients with mechanically plausible, moderate MP levels. The primary outcome YY is an indicator of in-hospital mortality. We include a rich set of baseline and early clinical variables as potential effect modifiers and confounders capturing patient severity and ventilator management, such as demographics, SAPS II score, smoking status, ARDS severity, vasopressor use, oxygenation and gas-exchange measures (e.g., PaO2, PaCO2, PaO2/FiO2), blood pressure, and ventilator settings from the first ICU day. After complete-case selection the analytical sample comprised n=5,011n=5{,}011 patients. In this analysis, our goal is to characterize how a 1 J/min decrease or increase in MP would change the risk of in-hospital mortality as a function of 𝑿\bm{X}, via the nudge effect τδ​(a,𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x}) and the corresponding CMTP effect τδ​(𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x}). This identifies clinically-relevant effect modifiers that drive heterogeneous benefits or harms of modest changes in MP. We present results for shifts δ∈{−1,+1}\delta\in\{-1,\,+1\} J/min; the negative shift corresponds to a modest reduction and the positive shift to a modest increase in MP.

Across all estimators and loss specifications, Figure 2 shows that the intercept, which is interpretable as the predicted effect of the shift at the population-mean covariate profile, is small in absolute magnitude and negative under δ=−1\delta=-1, with the sign reversing under δ=+1\delta=+1, indicating that a modest 1 J/min reduction in MP is associated with a slight decrease in the probability of in-hospital mortality at the population level. The figure displays the top 20 covariates ranked by their mean absolute CMTP coefficient across all six estimator combinations (three loss specifications ×\times two CMTP constructions). The ranking and direction of the leading effect modifiers are broadly consistent across methods, suggesting that the substantive conclusions are robust to the choice of estimator. Full coefficient estimates and standard errors for the A-learning CMTP estimators under all three loss specifications are reported in Supplementary Tables S4 and S5. bA-learning and overlap weighting (Supplentary Figure S2) yield closely aligned estimates in direction and magnitude, consistent with targeting the same population projection under correct nuisance specification, whereas the density-ratio estimator (Supplementary Figure S3) shows substantially wider spread, reflecting its greater sensitivity to density-model misspecification and the stabilization correction.

The maximum arterial pH on ICU day 1 (ph_max_day1) emerges as the single strongest and most consistent effect modifier across all estimation strategies and both shift directions. Under δ=−1\delta=-1 J/min, its CMTP coefficient is negative across all methods: a higher maximum pH is associated with a greater predicted reduction in mortality probability from lowering MP. Under the symmetric positive shift δ=+1\delta=+1 J/min, the coefficient reverses sign. Clinically, a high blood pH on day 1 often indicates respiratory alkalosis from the ventilator giving more support than needed, so slightly reducing the ventilator’s power lowers unnecessary strain without harming breathing. In contrast, patients with low pH usually need the extra ventilator support (for example, due to acid buildup or poor carbon dioxide removal), and reducing the power does not help and may even be harmful. Overall, reducing ventilator intensity may work best for patients who do not rely on it to correct serious breathing or metabolic problems.

Supplementary Figure S4 displays the mean nudge effect τ^δ​(Ai,𝑿i)=δ⋅(β^A+𝑿i⊤​β^A​X)\hat{\tau}_{\delta}(A_{i},\bm{X}_{i})=\delta\cdot(\hat{\beta}_{A}+\bm{X}_{i}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{AX}) averaged within deciles of the observed MP distribution, for the A-learning squared-loss model with augmentation. For δ=−1\delta=-1 J/min, all deciles save the highest show negative mean nudge effects, indicating a predicted benefit from power reduction, and for δ=+1\delta=+1 J/min the mirror image obtains. Because the nudge model is linear in AA, variation across power deciles reflects systematic differences in the covariate profiles 𝑿i\bm{X}_{i} of patients who receive different power levels, rather than a dose-response gradient in the nudge itself: the lowest deciles are enriched for higher pH and elective service types (most negative nudge), while the highest decile is enriched for severely ill patients with low pH and vasopressor dependence (near-zero nudge).

7 Discussion

Continuous treatments arise in many clinical and policy settings, where the scientific question is often not simply whether treatment works, but how much treatment should be delivered, and for whom. Most existing methods for continuous treatments focus on ADRFs or CADRFs, which require positivity over the entire treatment range. In clinical observational studies, treatment values are often chosen based on patient severity, contraindications, protocols, and physician judgment, so many doses are rarely observed for certain patient profiles, and estimating the ADRF or CADRF surfaces will require extrapolation to covariate regions with little or no support.

Our framework targets local incremental effects through the conditional nudge effect and CMTP rather than global dose-response curves. Although related ideas appear in work on stochastic interventions and modified treatment policies, they have not been developed systematically for heterogeneous effects of continuous treatments. Because the estimands are anchored to observed treatment values, they require only local, shift-specific overlap rather than positivity across the full dose range. We use a duplicated-arm construction that translates the continuous shift problem to a two-arm contrast between the observed and shifted doses, enabling weighting and A-learning losses for both estimands. Under unrestricted function classes for the effects, we show that the population losses identify the causal effects. Under finite-dimensional bases for the effects, they identify corresponding projections of the nudge or CMTP onto the working model. Notably, the direct CMTP estimator requires only the shift-specific exchangeability condition (Assumption 3(A′)), which is strictly weaker than the exchangeability condition needed to identify the full nudge surface, so the direct approach is valid even when the conditional nudge effect itself is not identified. We show augmentation can improve precision by subtracting an outcome regression without changing the population target.

Our simulations demonstrate that the proposed estimators recover the relevant projected targets as sample size increases, and that augmentation generally improves precision. The mechanical ventilation analysis illustrates the practical value of the framework. Rather than focusing on the entire CADRF, our approach can assess which patient characteristics yield benefit or harm from a modest change in MP. This type of local treatment effect question is relevant for individualized clinical decision-making. Our asymptotic theory uses Donsker and smoothness conditions for nuisance estimators. Extensions using cross-fitting and double machine learning are straightforward and would allow more general machine-learning nuisance fits. Use of finite-dimensional bases yields projection parameters unless the working model of the effect is correctly specified, so growing spline or sieve bases are a natural approach for reducing approximation error. Finally, the shift magnitude δ\delta should be chosen to balance clinical relevance with empirical overlap. Future work could develop diagnostics for feasible shift selection as in Jiang and Huling (2025), extend our framework to longitudinal continuous treatments, and provide simultaneous inference for richer effect-modification summaries.

A Additional Methodological Concepts

A.1 Direct CMTP Estimation via Weighting

Here, we work with the weighting loss for directly estimating the CMTP. This loss is analogous to the weighting loss in (2) in Section 2.3.1, integrated over the distribution of AΛA_{\Lambda} given 𝑿=𝒙\bm{X}=\bm{x}. For a measurable function f:𝒳→ℝf:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}, we define the direct weighting CMTP loss

ℓWCMTP​(f)=𝔼⁡[w⁡(𝑿,AΛ,Λ)​{Y−Λ​f​(𝑿)}2|X],\ell_{W}^{\mathrm{CMTP}}(f)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[w(\bm{X},A_{\Lambda},\Lambda)\,\big\{Y-\Lambda f(\bm{X})\big\}^{2}\;\middle|\;X\right],

where w⁡(𝑿,AΛ,Λ)w(\bm{X},A_{\Lambda},\Lambda) is any nonnegative arm weight as described earlier. For fixed 𝒙\bm{x}, differentiating ℓWCMTP​(f)\ell_{W}^{\mathrm{CMTP}}(f) with respect to f⁡(𝒙)f(\bm{x}) yields the first-order condition 𝔼⁡[w⁡(𝑿,AΛ,Λ)​Λ​{Y−Λ​f​(𝑿)}|𝑿=𝒙]=0,\mathbb{E}\big[w(\bm{X},A_{\Lambda},\Lambda)\,\Lambda\{Y-\Lambda f(\bm{X})\}\,\big|\,\bm{X}=\bm{x}\big]=0, so that the pointwise minimizer takes the ratio form

f∗​(𝒙)=𝔼⁡[w⁡(𝑿,AΛ,Λ)​Λ​Y∣𝑿=𝒙]𝔼⁡[w⁡(𝑿,AΛ,Λ)​Λ2∣𝑿=𝒙]=NW​(𝒙)DW​(𝒙),f^{*}(\bm{x})=\frac{\mathbb{E}\big[w(\bm{X},A_{\Lambda},\Lambda)\,\Lambda Y\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}\big]}{\mathbb{E}\big[w(\bm{X},A_{\Lambda},\Lambda)\,\Lambda^{2}\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}\big]}=\frac{N_{W}(\bm{x})}{D_{W}(\bm{x})},

where we write NW​(𝒙):=𝔼⁡[w⁡(𝑿,AΛ,Λ)​Λ​Y∣𝑿=𝒙], and ​DW​(𝒙):=𝔼⁡[w⁡(𝑿,AΛ,Λ)​Λ2∣𝑿=𝒙].N_{W}(\bm{x}):=\mathbb{E}\big[w(\bm{X},A_{\Lambda},\Lambda)\,\Lambda Y\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}\big],\text{ and }D_{W}(\bm{x}):=\mathbb{E}\big[w(\bm{X},A_{\Lambda},\Lambda)\,\Lambda^{2}\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}\big]. Subsequent calculations below make these terms explicit for the overlap and density-ratio weighting schemes.

We define the arm contrast μΔ​(a,𝐱):=μ⁡(a+δ,𝐱)−μ⁡(a,𝐱).\mu_{\Delta}(a,\bm{x}):=\mu(a+\delta,\bm{x})-\mu(a,\bm{x}). Then:

We are given that Y|(A,𝑿)Y\mid(A,\bm{X}) follow a canonical exponential family with NLL MM and mean function μ​(𝜼)=b′​(𝜼)\mu({\bm{\eta}})=b^{\prime}({\bm{\eta}}), and consider the duplicated-arm construction (AΛ,Λ)(A_{\Lambda},\Lambda) with Λ∈{12,−12}\Lambda\in\{\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\} as in Section 2.3. ℓWNLL(f;a,𝒙)=𝔼[w(a,𝒙,Λ)M(Y,Λf(a,𝒙))|𝑿=𝒙,AΛ=a].\ell_{W}^{\mathrm{NLL}}(f;a,\bm{x})=\mathbb{E}\Big[w(a,\bm{x},\Lambda)\,M\bigl(Y,\Lambda f(a,\bm{x})\bigr)\,\Big|\,\bm{X}=\bm{x},\ A_{\Lambda}=a\Big]. (10)

𝔼[ω(a,𝒙,Λ)Λ{μ(Λf(a,𝒙))−Y}|𝑿=𝒙,AΛ=a]=0,\mathbb{E}\Big[\omega(a,\bm{x},\Lambda)\,\Lambda\,\bigl\{\mu\bigl(\Lambda f(a,\bm{x})\bigr)-Y\bigr\}\,\Big|\,\bm{X}=\bm{x},\ A_{\Lambda}=a\Big]=0, (11)

where, for the canonical NLL, ω⁡(a,𝒙,Λ)=w⁡(a,𝒙,Λ)\omega(a,\bm{x},\Lambda)=w(a,\bm{x},\Lambda) exactly, since ∂M⁡(y,η)/∂η=μ⁡(η)−y\partial M(y,\eta)/\partial\eta=\mu(\eta)-y.
