A.3 Direct CMTP Estimation via NLL Loss

In the exponential-family framework of Section 2.5, the direct CMTP estimators from Section 2.4 can be extended by replacing the squared-error criteria with the corresponding canonical NLL. Rather than modeling a local nudge effect at a fixed dose aa, we now posit a link-scale CMTP contrast f:𝒳→ℝf:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} that depends only on the covariates 𝑿\bm{X} and is evaluated under the duplicated-arm mixture for AΛA_{\Lambda} given 𝑿\bm{X}. In both the weighting and A-learning formulations, a natural first step is to take the corresponding nudge NLL loss (from (10) and (9)), simply replacing the local contrast f⁡(a,𝒙)f(a,\bm{x}) by a function f⁡(𝒙)f(\bm{x}) and conditioning only on XX. However, exactly as in the squared-error case in Lemma 1 and Lemma 3, the resulting first-order conditions show that the population minimizer f∗​(𝒙)f^{*}(\bm{x}) does not recover the CMTP τδ​(𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x}) directly. Instead, the numerator of f∗​(𝒙)f^{*}(\bm{x}) involves an average of the arm-specific mean shift μ⁡(a+δ,𝒙)−μ⁡(a,𝒙)\mu(a+\delta,\bm{x})-\mu(a,\bm{x}) weighted by a method-specific factor hM​(𝒙,a)h_{M}(\bm{x},a) that depends on the arm propensity πΛ​(𝒙,a)\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a) and the curvature of the NLL, while the denominator averages the same hM​(𝒙,a)h_{M}(\bm{x},a) alone. Thus, the unstabilized NLL losses identify a weighted CMTP of the form

f∗​(𝒙)=𝔼⁡[hM​(𝑿,AΛ)​{μ⁡(AΛ+δ,𝑿)−μ⁡(AΛ,𝑿)}∣𝑿=𝒙]𝔼⁡[hM​(𝑿,AΛ)∣𝑿=𝒙],f^{*}(\bm{x})=\frac{\mathbb{E}\!\big[h_{M}(\bm{X},A_{\Lambda})\{\mu(A_{\Lambda}+\delta,\bm{X})-\mu(A_{\Lambda},\bm{X})\}\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}\big]}{\mathbb{E}\!\big[h_{M}(\bm{X},A_{\Lambda})\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}\big]},

with hMh_{M} taking different but explicit forms for overlap, density-ratio, and A-learning variants, rather than the unweighted CMTP τδ​(𝒙)=𝔼⁡[μ⁡(A+δ,𝒙)−μ⁡(A,x)∣𝑿=𝒙]\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x})=\mathbb{E}[\mu(A+\delta,\bm{x})-\mu(A,x)\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}]. To target τδ​(𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x}) itself, we therefore stabilize the direct NLL losses by dividing each duplicated observation’s contribution by hM​(𝑿,AΛ)/{1−πΛ​(𝑿,AΛ)}h_{M}(\bm{X},A_{\Lambda})/\{1-\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{X},A_{\Lambda})\}. The additional factor 1−πΛ1-\pi_{\Lambda} is essential: as in the squared-error case (see Proposition 5 of the main paper), the expectations above are taken under the duplicated-arm mixture law of AΛA_{\Lambda} given 𝑿\bm{X}, and the identity {1−πΛ​(𝒙,a)}​fAΛ|𝑿​(a∣𝒙)=12​gA|𝑿​(a∣𝒙)\{1-\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a)\}f_{A_{\Lambda}\mid\bm{X}}(a\mid\bm{x})=\tfrac{1}{2}g_{A\mid\bm{X}}(a\mid\bm{x}) converts the mixture average into an average over the natural law of AA given 𝑿\bm{X}. With this stabilization, the implicit weighting cancels in both the numerator and denominator of f∗​(𝒙)f^{*}(\bm{x}), so that the unique minimizer of the stabilized NLL loss coincides with the CMTP τδ​(𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x}) on the appropriate scale (mean scale for squared error, link scale for NLL). For the A-learning estimator, hM=πΛ​(1−πΛ)h_{M}=\pi_{\Lambda}(1-\pi_{\Lambda}) and the stabilizer reduces to πΛ​(𝑿,AΛ)\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{X},A_{\Lambda}). As in the squared-loss setting, one can also subtract an arbitrary function m⁡(A,𝑿)m(A,\bm{X}) inside the NLL to form augmented versions of these stabilized losses. At the population level this only recenters the first order conditions and does not change the fact that τδ​(𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x}) is the target of estimation, while yielding variance-reduction benefits in finite and large samples. Detailed derivations of the direct CMTP losses for the logistic case may be found in the proof of Theorem 4 in Section D.

A.4 Additional Empirical Loss Functions

Let w^iλ:=w^​(Ai−λ​δ,𝑿i,λ)\widehat{w}_{i}^{\lambda}:=\widehat{w}(A_{i}-\lambda\delta,\bm{X}_{i},\lambda), where the third argument λ∈{0,1}\lambda\in\{0,1\} indicates the duplicated arm (corresponding to Λ=λ−12\Lambda=\lambda-\tfrac{1}{2} in the population weight of (2)). The estimated weighting functions w^iλ\widehat{w}_{i}^{\lambda} may be obtained from the original sample {Ai,𝑿i}i=1n\{A_{i},\bm{X}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} when density-ratio weights are used, or from the duplicated sample when overlap or IPW weights are used. The conditional nudge effect function is obtained by minimizing

t^δ,W=arg​mintδ∈𝒯⁡ℙnΛ​w^iλ​{Yi−(λ−12)​tδ​(𝒁iλ)}2.\widehat{t}_{\delta,W}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{t_{\delta}\in\mathcal{T}}\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\Lambda}\widehat{w}_{i}^{\lambda}\left\{Y_{i}-{\bigl(\lambda-\tfrac{1}{2}\bigr)\,}t_{\delta}(\bm{Z}_{i}^{\lambda})\right\}^{2}.

The factor λ−12\lambda-\tfrac{1}{2} is the arm coding Λ\Lambda of the population loss (2); omitting it would yield an unweighted regression of YY on the basis, which targets the average of the two arm means rather than their contrast. If tδt_{\delta} is represented in a linear basis, tδ​(a,𝒙)=𝜽⊤​𝒃​(a,𝒙),t_{\delta}(a,\bm{x})=\bm{\theta}^{\top}\bm{b}(a,\bm{x}), then t^δ,W​(a,𝒙)=𝜽^W⊤​𝒃​(a,𝒙)\widehat{t}_{\delta,W}(a,\bm{x})=\widehat{\bm{\theta}}_{W}^{\top}\bm{b}(a,\bm{x}), where

𝜽^W=arg​min𝜽⁡ℙnΛ​w^iλ​{Yi−(λ−12)​𝜽⊤​𝒃iλ}2={14​ℙnΛ​w^iλ​𝒃iλ​𝒃iλ⊤}−1​{12​ℙnΛ​(2​λ−1)​w^iλ​𝒃iλ​Yi}.\displaystyle\widehat{\bm{\theta}}_{W}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\bm{\theta}}\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\Lambda}\widehat{w}_{i}^{\lambda}\left\{Y_{i}-{\bigl(\lambda-\tfrac{1}{2}\bigr)}\bm{\theta}^{\top}{\bm{b}}_{i}^{\lambda}\right\}^{2}=\left\{{\tfrac{1}{4}}\,\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\Lambda}\widehat{w}_{i}^{\lambda}{\bm{b}}_{i}^{\lambda}{\bm{b}}_{i}^{\lambda\top}\right\}^{-1}\left\{{\tfrac{1}{2}}\,\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\Lambda}{(2\lambda-1)}\,\widehat{w}_{i}^{\lambda}{\bm{b}}_{i}^{\lambda}Y_{i}\right\}.

Thus the weighting estimator can be implemented by standard weighted least squares on the duplicated sample.

Lemma 4 (Population limits of linear-basis nudge estimators for weighting).

Let τδ​(a,𝐱)\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x}) denote the conditional nudge effect and suppose we approximate it in a linear basis, τδ​(a,𝐱)≈𝛉⊤​𝐛​(a,𝐱),\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x})\approx\bm{\theta}^{\top}\bm{b}(a,\bm{x}), where 𝐛⁡(a,𝐱)∈ℝp\bm{b}(a,\bm{x})\in\mathbb{R}^{p} is a fixed vector of basis functions and 𝛉∈ℝp\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} is unknown. Suppose the weights are strictly positive, satisfy the balancing condition (3), and w^\widehat{w} is uniformly consistent for ww; suppose also the limiting Gram matrix below is nonsingular. Then 𝛉^W→𝛉W∗\widehat{\bm{\theta}}_{W}\to\bm{\theta}_{W}^{*} in probability, where, with hW​(a,𝐱):=πΛ​(𝐱,a)​w​(a,𝐱,12)h_{W}(a,\bm{x}):=\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a)\,w(a,\bm{x},\tfrac{1}{2}),

𝜽W∗=arg​min𝜽∈ℝp𝔼[hW(AΛ,𝑿){τδ(AΛ,𝑿)−𝜽⊤𝒃(AΛ,𝑿)}2]Λ,\bm{\theta}_{W}^{*}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}}\mathbb{E}{{}^{\Lambda}}\left[h_{W}({A_{\Lambda}},\bm{X})\left\{\tau_{\delta}({A_{\Lambda}},\bm{X})-\bm{\theta}^{\top}\bm{b}({A_{\Lambda}},\bm{X})\right\}^{2}\right]{,}

where 𝔼Λ\mathbb{E}^{\Lambda} denotes expectation under the duplicated-arm law of (AΛ,𝐗)(A_{\Lambda},\bm{X}), as in Lemma 2 of the main paper.

Proof.

The argument parallels the proof of Lemma 2 in the main paper: with the arm coding included, 𝔼[w(Λ~−12)2∣AΛ,𝑿]=14{w+πΛ+w−(1−πΛ)}=12πΛw+\mathbb{E}[w\,(\widetilde{\Lambda}-\tfrac{1}{2})^{2}\mid A_{\Lambda},\bm{X}]=\tfrac{1}{4}\{w_{+}\pi_{\Lambda}+w_{-}(1-\pi_{\Lambda})\}=\tfrac{1}{2}\,\pi_{\Lambda}w_{+} and 𝔼[w(Λ~−12)Y∣AΛ,𝑿]=12πΛw+τδ(AΛ,𝑿)\mathbb{E}[w\,(\widetilde{\Lambda}-\tfrac{1}{2})Y\mid A_{\Lambda},\bm{X}]=\tfrac{1}{2}\,\pi_{\Lambda}w_{+}\,\tau_{\delta}(A_{\Lambda},\bm{X}) under the balancing condition and the conditions of Proposition 1; the limit then follows from the law of large numbers, uniform consistency of w^\widehat{w}, and the continuous mapping theorem. ∎

In particular, for overlap weights ww, one has hW​(a,𝒙)=πΛ​(𝒙,a)​{1−πΛ​(𝒙,a)},h_{W}(a,\bm{x})=\pi_{\Lambda}({\bm{x},a})\{1-\pi_{\Lambda}({\bm{x},a})\}, so the A-learning and overlap-weighting estimators project τδ\tau_{\delta} onto the same basis with the same weight function; for IPW weights hW≡1h_{W}\equiv 1, and for density-ratio weights hW=1−πΛh_{W}=1-\pi_{\Lambda}.

B Additional Simulation Results

First, we report the inference results of nudge estimation below in Table 2. Next, in Section B.1 we introduce a new simulation experiment that studies the performance of the proposed methods under the logistic loss.

B.1 Logistic Loss

In a second simulation, we consider a binary outcome under a correctly specified logistic model, so effects are defined on the log-odds scale. We evaluate whether the proposed weighting and A-learning estimators of the conditional nudge and CMTP effects remain approximately unbiased under a nonlinear link, and compare direct CMTP estimation with averaging the estimated nudge under logistic loss. Unlike in the linear setting, we omit outcome-regression augmentation so that differences reflect only the loss and CMTP construction. To facilitate comparison with Setup 1, we retain the same covariate and treatment distributions. We generate i.i.d. covariates 𝑿=(X1,X2)⊤\bm{X}=(X_{1},X_{2})^{\top}, where X1∼Unif⁡(−1,1)X_{1}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(-1,1) and X2∼Bernoulli⁡(0.7)X_{2}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(0.7), independently. Conditional on 𝑿\bm{X}, A|𝑿∼Exp​{λ⁡(𝑿)}A\mid\bm{X}\sim\mathrm{Exp}\{\lambda(\bm{X})\}, where λ⁡(𝑿)=exp⁡{−(2+0.5​X1+X2)}\lambda(\bm{X})=\exp\{-(2+0.5X_{1}+X_{2})\}, so that 𝔼⁡[A∣𝑿=𝒙]=exp⁡(2+0.5​x1+x2)\mathbb{E}[A\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}]=\exp(2+0.5x_{1}+x_{2}). Given (A,𝑿)(A,\bm{X}), we generate Y|(A,𝑿)∼Bernoulli⁡{μ⁡(A,𝑿)}Y\mid(A,\bm{X})\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}\{\mu(A,\bm{X})\}, with μ⁡(A,𝑿)=expit⁡{η⁡(A,𝑿)}\mu(A,\bm{X})=\operatorname{expit}\{\eta(A,\bm{X})\}, where η⁡(A,𝑿)\eta(A,\bm{X}) has the form as in Section 5, with δ=0.5\delta=0.5, α=−1.5\alpha=-1.5, β=2.0\beta=2.0, βA=−0.50\beta_{A}=-0.50, and βA​X=0.25\beta_{AX}=0.25. This model specification induces a nonlinear, covariate-modified treatment effect on the log-odds scale while a parametric structure that allows for closed-form nudge and CMTP effects.

The conditional nudge effect is defined on the log-odds scale as τδ​(a,𝒙)=η⁡(a+δ,𝒙)−η⁡(a,𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x})=\eta(a+\delta,\bm{x})-\eta(a,\bm{x}), corresponding to an odds ratio exp⁡{τδ​(a,𝒙)}\exp\{\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x})\} under the shift a↦a+δa\mapsto a+\delta. Under a polynomial working model, this contrast has the same form as that in Section 5 and with coefficients interpreted on the log-odds scale. The CMTP effect averages this contrast over the observed conditional treatment distribution, namely τδ​(𝒙)=𝔼⁡{τδ​(A,𝑿)∣𝑿=𝒙}\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x})=\mathbb{E}\{\tau_{\delta}(A,\bm{X})\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}\}, where 𝔼⁡[A∣𝑿=𝒙]=exp⁡(2+0.5​x1+x2)\mathbb{E}[A\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}]=\exp(2+0.5x_{1}+x_{2}). As in the linear setting, we summarize τδ​(𝒙)\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x}) by its least-squares projection onto the span of {1,X1,X2}\{1,X_{1},X_{2}\}. The resulting coefficients then define the CMTP parameter on the log-odds scale.

The estimators here parallel those in Setup 1 but use logistic rather than squared error loss and for simplicity regression augmentation. Density, Overlap, and A-learning approaches are each fit under a linear working model for the log-odds contrast, and for the CMTP we again compare the “average” and “direct” constructions, yielding six distinct CMTP estimators. As in Setup 1, for n∈{500,1000,5000}n\in\{500,1000,5000\} we generate R=200R=200 independent datasets and compute empirical bias and root mean squared error relative to the known polynomial nudge coefficients and projected CMTP coefficients.

Figure 3 displays the root integrated mean squared error of the estimated nudge (left) and CMTP (right) functions: error decreases with nn for all methods, and the direct CMTP estimators attain uniformly lower error than their averaging counterparts in this design. Supplementary Tables 3 and 4 report coefficient-level bias, RMSE and 95% Wald coverage for the logistic estimators under the nudge and CMTP models.

C Additional Details and Results for the Mechanical Power Data Analysis

This section provides the full list of candidate effect modifiers used in Section 6 of the main paper, coefficient estimates under the overlap and density-ratio weighting schemes (Figures 4 and 5), and full coefficient tables with standard errors for the A-learning CMTP estimators (Tables 5 and 6).

Effect modifiers.

We consider a rich set of p=24p=24 pre-treatment covariates 𝑿i∈𝒳⊂ℝp\bm{X}_{i}\in\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{p} measured on ICU day 1, comprising:

  • •

    Demographics and severity: sex, Simplified Acute Physiology Score II (SAPS II), smoking history.

  • •

    Respiratory mechanics: minimum and maximum respiratory rate, minimum and maximum peak inspiratory pressure, plateau pressure, fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2).

  • •

    Gas exchange: minimum and maximum partial pressure of arterial oxygen (PaO2), PaO2/FiO2 ratio, minimum and maximum partial pressure of arterial carbon dioxide (PaCO2), minimum and maximum arterial pH.

  • •

    Haemodynamics and organ support: minimum mean arterial blood pressure, vasopressor use on day 1.

  • •

    Admission characteristics: primary ICU service (cardiac surgery, cardiac medical, general medical, neurological medical, neurological surgical, oncological medical, orthopaedic, plastic surgery, thoracic surgery, trauma, vascular surgery, and other), insurance category (Medicaid, Medicare, private, self-pay), ARDS severity classification and its missingness indicator.

  • •

    Comorbidities: asthma.

Categorical variables were expanded into K−1K-1 dummy variable columns and constant columns were removed. Continuous covariates were mean-centered prior to analysis so that all CMTP coefficients represent deviations from the population-mean covariate profile and the model intercept is interpretable as the predicted nudge effect at the population-mean.

D Proofs

D.1 Proofs of Propositions

Proof of Proposition 1.

Fix 𝒙∈𝒳\bm{x}\in\mathcal{X} and a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A} with fA|𝑿​(a∣𝒙)>0f_{A\mid\bm{X}}(a\mid\bm{x})>0; Assumption 2 then guarantees fA|𝑿​(a+δ∣𝒙)>0f_{A\mid\bm{X}}(a+\delta\mid\bm{x})>0, so both conditional means below are well defined. By consistency (Assumption 1),

𝔼[Y∣𝑿=𝒙,A=a+δ]=𝔼{Y(a+δ)∣𝑿=𝒙,A=a+δ},\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x},A=a+\delta]=\mathbb{E}\{Y(a+\delta)\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x},A=a+\delta\},
𝔼[Y∣𝑿=𝒙,A=a]=𝔼{Y(a)∣𝑿=𝒙,A=a}.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x},A=a]=\mathbb{E}\{Y(a)\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x},A=a\}.

By Assumption 3(A′) with q⁡(a,𝒙)=a+δq(a,\bm{x})=a+\delta,

𝔼{Y(a+δ)∣𝑿=𝒙,A=a+δ}=𝔼{Y(a+δ)∣𝑿=𝒙,A=a}.\mathbb{E}\{Y(a+\delta)\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x},A=a+\delta\}=\mathbb{E}\{Y(a+\delta)\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x},A=a\}.

Subtracting the two consistency identities and applying the display above,

𝔼[Y∣𝑿=𝒙,A=a+δ]−𝔼[Y∣𝑿=𝒙,A=a]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x},A=a+\delta]-\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x},A=a] =𝔼{Y(a+δ)−Y(a)∣𝑿=𝒙,A=a}\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\{Y(a+\delta)-Y(a)\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x},A=a\}
=𝔼⁡{Y⁡(a+δ)−Y⁡(a)∣𝑿=𝒙}\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\{Y(a+\delta)-Y(a)\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}\}
=τδ​(a,𝒙),\displaystyle=\tau_{\delta}(a,\bm{x}),

where the second equality is Assumption 3(A). Note that the proof makes it clear where each condition is used: (A′) moves the shifted-arm potential outcome across conditioning arms, while (A) removes the dose from the conditioning set in the contrast. ∎

Proof of Proposition 2.

Fix 𝒙\bm{x} with f𝑿​(𝒙)>0f_{\bm{X}}(\bm{x})>0 and write m0(a,𝒙)=𝔼[Y∣𝑿=𝒙,A=a]m_{0}(a,\bm{x})=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x},A=a] for the observed outcome regression. By consistency (Assumption 1), Y=Y⁡(A)Y=Y(A) almost surely, so

𝔼⁡{Y⁡(A)∣𝑿=𝒙}=𝔼⁡[Y∣𝑿=𝒙].\mathbb{E}\{Y(A)\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}\}=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}].

Next, by the tower property,

𝔼{Y(A+δ)∣𝑿=𝒙}=𝔼[𝔼{Y(A+δ)∣𝑿=𝒙,A}|𝑿=𝒙].\mathbb{E}\{Y(A+\delta)\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}\}=\mathbb{E}\big[\,\mathbb{E}\{Y(A+\delta)\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x},A\}\,\big|\,\bm{X}=\bm{x}\big].

𝔼{Y(a+δ)∣𝑿=𝒙,A=a}\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\{Y(a+\delta)\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x},A=a\} =𝔼{Y(a+δ)∣𝑿=𝒙,A=a+δ}\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\{Y(a+\delta)\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x},A=a+\delta\}
=𝔼[Y∣𝑿=𝒙,A=a+δ]=m0(a+δ,𝒙).\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x},A=a+\delta]=m_{0}(a+\delta,\bm{x}).

Hence 𝔼⁡{Y⁡(A+δ)∣𝑿=𝒙}=𝔼⁡[m0​(A+δ,𝒙)∣𝑿=𝒙]\mathbb{E}\{Y(A+\delta)\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}\}=\mathbb{E}[m_{0}(A+\delta,\bm{x})\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}], and subtracting the two identities gives

Step 4 (augmentation invariance). For the augmented stabilized loss (8), the first-order condition involves Y−m⁡(AΛ,𝑿)Y-m(A_{\Lambda},\bm{X}) instead of YY in the numerator. Remark 1.

The following remark is restated from the main paper’s Section 4 (where it now appears in abbreviated form). We next translate the asymptotic normality of the conditional nudge estimator into inference for the plug-in CMTP estimator obtained by averaging the fitted nudge over the conditional distribution of A|𝑿=𝒙A\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}.

Corollary 1 (Asymptotic normality of plug-in CMTP from A-learning nudge estimator).

If instead only ‖𝐛¯^​(𝐱)−𝐛¯​(𝐱)‖=op​(1)\|\widehat{\bar{\bm{b}}}(\bm{x})-\bar{\bm{b}}(\bm{x})\|=o_{p}(1), then τ^δplug(𝐱)−τδ(𝐱)=Op(n−1/2)+Op(∥𝐛¯^(𝐱)−𝐛¯(𝐱)∥)\widehat{\tau}_{\delta}^{\,\mathrm{plug}}(\bm{x})-\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x})=O_{p}(n^{-1/2})+O_{p}\big(\|\widehat{\bar{\bm{b}}}(\bm{x})-\bar{\bm{b}}(\bm{x})\|\big), so the plug-in estimator inherits the (possibly slower) rate of 𝐛¯^​(𝐱)\widehat{\bar{\bm{b}}}(\bm{x}); in particular, generic nonparametric or cross-fitted estimators of 𝐛¯​(𝐱)\bar{\bm{b}}(\bm{x}) converge more slowly than n\sqrt{n}, and the display above then no longer describes the limiting distribution.

Thus, Corollary 1 shows that when 𝒃¯​(𝒙)\bar{\bm{b}}(\bm{x}) can be estimated faster than root-nn in rate, e.g. when the treatment’s distribution is known by design, the plug-in CMTP estimator inherits the root-nn asymptotic normality of the estimator of the nudge effect coefficients. When 𝒃¯​(𝒙)\bar{\bm{b}}(\bm{x}) is instead estimated nonparametrically, the plug-in estimator converges at the slower rate of 𝒃¯^​(𝒙)\widehat{\bar{\bm{b}}}(\bm{x}) and the stated limiting normal distribution no longer applies. Remark 2 describes the same-sample projection implementation we use in practice, which explicitly accounts for the additional averaging step.

Remark 2 (Same-sample projection implementation).

In practice (Section 2 of the main paper) we project the fitted nudge onto a basis 𝐜⁡(𝐱)\bm{c}(\bm{x}) using the same sample, i.e., 𝛃^plug={ℙn​𝐜i​𝐜i⊤}−1​ℙn​𝐜i​𝐛​(Ai,𝐗i)⊤​𝛉^A\widehat{\bm{\beta}}^{\mathrm{plug}}=\{\mathbb{P}_{n}\bm{c}_{i}\bm{c}_{i}^{\top}\}^{-1}\mathbb{P}_{n}\bm{c}_{i}\,\bm{b}(A_{i},\bm{X}_{i})^{\top}\widehat{\bm{\theta}}_{A}, which targets 𝛃∗=𝐌​𝛉A∗\bm{\beta}^{*}=\bm{M}\bm{\theta}_{A}^{*} with 𝐌:={𝔼⁡(𝐜​𝐜⊤)}−1​𝔼​{𝐜​𝐛​(A,𝐗)⊤}\bm{M}:=\{\mathbb{E}(\bm{c}\bm{c}^{\top})\}^{-1}\mathbb{E}\{\bm{c}\,\bm{b}(A,\bm{X})^{\top}\}; under the conditions of Corollary 1, 𝛃∗\bm{\beta}^{*} is the L2​(P𝐗)L_{2}(P_{\bm{X}}) projection coefficient of τδ​(𝐗)\tau_{\delta}(\bm{X}) onto 𝐜⁡(𝐗)\bm{c}(\bm{X}). Averaging the fitted nudge over the same sample contributes an additional empirical-process term to the influence function: under (C1)-(C3), finite fourth moments of (𝐛,𝐜)(\bm{b},\bm{c}), and nonsingular 𝔼⁡(𝐜​𝐜⊤)\mathbb{E}(\bm{c}\bm{c}^{\top}), n​(𝛃^plug−𝛃∗)↝N⁡(𝟎,𝔼⁡{h​(𝐎)⊗2})\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\bm{\beta}}^{\mathrm{plug}}-\bm{\beta}^{*})\rightsquigarrow N\big(\bm{0},\ \mathbb{E}\{h(\bm{O})^{\otimes 2}\}\big), where

h⁡(𝑶)=𝑴​𝑫−1​ϕA​(𝑶)+{𝔼⁡(𝒄​𝒄⊤)}−1​𝒄​(𝑿)​{𝒃​(A,𝑿)⊤​𝜽A∗−𝒄​(𝑿)⊤​𝜷∗}.h(\bm{O})=\bm{M}\,\bm{D}^{-1}\phi_{A}(\bm{O})+\{\mathbb{E}(\bm{c}\bm{c}^{\top})\}^{-1}\bm{c}(\bm{X})\big\{\bm{b}(A,\bm{X})^{\top}\bm{\theta}_{A}^{*}-\bm{c}(\bm{X})^{\top}\bm{\beta}^{*}\big\}.

The second term is not asymptotically negligible in general and is correlated with the first; ignoring it (as a naive application of Corollary 1 would) misstates the asymptotic variance.

We now identify the limits of each ingredient. First, note that

ΨA,n​(𝜽A∗,𝜼∗)=ℙn​[ψA​(Z,𝜽A∗,𝜼∗)]=P⁡[ψA​(Z,𝜽A∗,𝜼∗)]+𝔾n​[ψA​(Z,𝜽A∗,𝜼∗)],\Psi_{A,n}(\bm{\theta}_{A}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*})=\mathbb{P}_{n}\bigl[\psi_{A}(Z;\bm{\theta}_{A}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*})\bigr]=P\bigl[\psi_{A}(Z;\bm{\theta}_{A}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*})\bigr]+\mathbb{G}_{n}\bigl[\psi_{A}(Z;\bm{\theta}_{A}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*})\bigr],

where PP denotes the true distribution and 𝔾n\mathbb{G}_{n} the empirical process. Since P⁡[ψA​(Z,𝜽A∗,𝜼∗)]=𝟎P[\psi_{A}(Z;\bm{\theta}_{A}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*})]=\bm{0} by the definition of 𝜽A∗\bm{\theta}_{A}^{*}, we obtain

n​ΨA,n​(𝜽A∗,𝜼∗)=𝔾n​[ψA​(Z,𝜽A∗,𝜼∗)]=Op​(1)\sqrt{n}\,\Psi_{A,n}(\bm{\theta}_{A}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*})=\mathbb{G}_{n}\bigl[\psi_{A}(Z;\bm{\theta}_{A}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*})\bigr]=O_{p}(1)

and, by the central limit theorem for Donsker classes,

𝔾n​[ψA​(Z,𝜽A∗,𝜼∗)]→𝑑N⁡(𝟎,𝚺~A,log​(𝜽A∗,𝜼∗)),\mathbb{G}_{n}\bigl[\psi_{A}(Z;\bm{\theta}_{A}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*})\bigr]\xrightarrow{d}N\bigl(\bm{0},\,\widetilde{\bm{\Sigma}}_{A,\log}(\bm{\theta}_{A}^{*};\bm{\eta}^{*})\bigr),

where

𝚺~A,log​(𝜽A∗,𝜼∗):=𝔼⁡[ψA​(Z,𝜽A∗,𝜼∗)⊗2].\widetilde{\bm{\Sigma}}_{A,\log}(\bm{\theta}_{A}^{*};\bm{\eta}^{*}):=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\psi_{A}(Z;\bm{\theta}_{A}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*})^{\otimes 2}\bigr].

Next, by (C1),

n​(𝜼^n−𝜼∗)=−J𝜼−1​𝔾n​[U𝜼​(𝑶,𝜼∗)]+op​(1),\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\bm{\eta}}_{n}-\bm{\eta}^{*})=-\,J_{\bm{\eta}}^{-1}\mathbb{G}_{n}\bigl[U_{\bm{\eta}}(\bm{O};\bm{\eta}^{*})\bigr]+o_{p}(1),

with asymptotic variance 𝑽𝜼\bm{V}_{\bm{\eta}} and influence function −J𝜼−1​U𝜼​(𝑶,𝜼∗)-J_{\bm{\eta}}^{-1}U_{\bm{\eta}}(\bm{O};\bm{\eta}^{*}). For the derivatives, observe that Ψ˙A,n,𝜽​(𝜽A∗,𝜼∗)\dot{\Psi}_{A,n,\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\theta}_{A}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*}) is

ℙn​[−{Λ~−πΛ​(A,𝑿,𝜼∗)}2​μ′​({Λ~−πΛ​(A,𝑿,𝜼∗)}​𝜽A∗⁣⊤​b​(A,𝑿))​b​(A,𝑿)​b​(A,𝑿)⊤]+op​(1),\mathbb{P}_{n}\Bigl[-\{\widetilde{\Lambda}-\pi_{\Lambda}(A,\bm{X};\bm{\eta}^{*})\}^{2}\mu^{\prime}\bigl(\{\widetilde{\Lambda}-\pi_{\Lambda}(A,\bm{X};\bm{\eta}^{*})\}\bm{\theta}_{A}^{*\top}b(A,\bm{X})\bigr)\,b(A,\bm{X})b(A,\bm{X})^{\top}\Bigr]+o_{p}(1),

where μ′​(u)=μ⁡(u)​{1−μ⁡(u)}\mu^{\prime}(u)=\mu(u)\{1-\mu(u)\}. By the law of large numbers,

Ψ˙A,n,𝜽​(𝜽A∗,𝜼∗)→𝑝−𝑫log,\dot{\Psi}_{A,n,\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\theta}_{A}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*})\;\xrightarrow{p}\;-\bm{D}_{\log},

with

𝑫log=𝔼⁡[{Λ~−πΛ​(A,𝑿,𝜼∗)}2​μ′​({Λ~−πΛ​(A,𝑿,𝜼∗)}​𝜽A∗⁣⊤​b​(A,𝑿))​b​(A,𝑿)​b​(A,𝑿)⊤],\bm{D}_{\log}=\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\{\widetilde{\Lambda}-\pi_{\Lambda}(A,\bm{X};\bm{\eta}^{*})\}^{2}\mu^{\prime}\bigl(\{\widetilde{\Lambda}-\pi_{\Lambda}(A,\bm{X};\bm{\eta}^{*})\}\bm{\theta}_{A}^{*\top}b(A,\bm{X})\bigr)\,b(A,\bm{X})b(A,\bm{X})^{\top}\Bigr],

which is nonsingular by assumption. Similarly,

Ψ˙A,n,𝜼​(𝜽A∗,𝜼∗)→𝑝𝑩log,\dot{\Psi}_{A,n,\bm{\eta}}(\bm{\theta}_{A}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*})\;\xrightarrow{p}\;\bm{B}_{\log},

where

𝑩log:=∂∂𝜼⊤​ΨA​(𝜽A∗,𝜼)|𝜼=𝜼∗=𝔼⁡[∂∂𝜼⊤​ψA​(Z,𝜽A∗,𝜼)|𝜼=𝜼∗].\bm{B}_{\log}:=\frac{\partial}{\partial\bm{\eta}^{\top}}\Psi_{A}(\bm{\theta}_{A}^{*},\bm{\eta})\Big|_{\bm{\eta}=\bm{\eta}^{*}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial\bm{\eta}^{\top}}\psi_{A}(Z;\bm{\theta}_{A}^{*},\bm{\eta})\Big|_{\bm{\eta}=\bm{\eta}^{*}}\right].

n​(𝜽^A,log−𝜽A∗)→𝑑N⁡(𝟎,𝑫log−1​𝚺A,log​(𝜽A∗,𝜼∗)​𝑫log−1),\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\bm{\theta}}_{A,\log}-\bm{\theta}_{A}^{*})\xrightarrow{d}N\bigl(\bm{0},\,\bm{D}_{\log}^{-1}\,\bm{\Sigma}_{A,\log}(\bm{\theta}_{A}^{*};\bm{\eta}^{*})\,\bm{D}_{\log}^{-1}\bigr),

with

𝚺A,log​(𝜽A∗,𝜼∗)=𝔼⁡[{ψA​(Z,𝜽A∗,𝜼∗)−𝑩log​J𝜼−1​U𝜼​(𝑶,𝜼∗)}⊗2].\bm{\Sigma}_{A,\log}(\bm{\theta}_{A}^{*};\bm{\eta}^{*})=\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\bigl\{\psi_{A}(Z;\bm{\theta}_{A}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*})-\bm{B}_{\log}\,J_{\bm{\eta}}^{-1}U_{\bm{\eta}}(\bm{O};\bm{\eta}^{*})\bigr\}^{\otimes 2}\Bigr].

Finally, when 𝜼^n\widehat{\bm{\eta}}_{n} is efficient for 𝜼∗\bm{\eta}^{*} with asymptotic variance 𝑽𝜼\bm{V}_{\bm{\eta}}, the usual variance reduction argument for two-step estimators (see, e.g., Pierce (1982)) implies that

where 𝚺~A,log​(𝜽A∗,𝜼∗):=𝔼⁡[ψA​(Z,𝜽A∗,𝜼∗)⊗2]\widetilde{\bm{\Sigma}}_{A,\log}(\bm{\theta}_{A}^{*};\bm{\eta}^{*}):=\mathbb{E}[\psi_{A}(Z;\bm{\theta}_{A}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*})^{\otimes 2}] is the covariance when πΛ​(A,𝑿)\pi_{\Lambda}(A,\bm{X}) is known. This completes the proof. ∎

The following theorem, relocated from the main paper to conserve space, gives the asymptotic normality result for the logistic direct CMTP A-learning estimator; it is referenced from Section 4 of the main paper.

Theorem 4 (Asymptotic normality of logistic direct CMTP A-learning).

Let Y∈{0,1}Y\in\{0,1\} and write μ⁡(v)=expit⁡(v)\mu(v)=\operatorname{expit}(v) and μ′​(v)=μ⁡(v)​{1−μ⁡(v)}\mu^{\prime}(v)=\mu(v)\{1-\mu(v)\}. Under the duplicated-arm construction, subject 𝐎i\bm{O}_{i} contributes the two rows 𝐙iλ=(Ai−λ​δ,𝐗i)\bm{Z}_{i}^{\lambda}=(A_{i}-\lambda\delta,\bm{X}_{i}) with arm indicator Λ~iλ=λ∈{0,1}\widetilde{\Lambda}_{i}^{\lambda}=\lambda\in\{0,1\}; write πiλ​(𝛈):=πΛ​(𝐙iλ,𝛈)\pi_{i}^{\lambda}(\bm{\eta}):=\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{Z}_{i}^{\lambda};\bm{\eta}) and giλ​(𝛈):=λ−πiλ​(𝛈)g_{i}^{\lambda}(\bm{\eta}):=\lambda-\pi_{i}^{\lambda}(\bm{\eta}). Let 𝐛i:=𝐛⁡(𝐗i)\bm{b}_{i}:=\bm{b}(\bm{X}_{i}) denote the column vector of basis functions in 𝐗\bm{X} only, used for the direct CMTP working model f⁡(𝐱)=𝛉⊤​𝐛​(𝐱)f(\bm{x})=\bm{\theta}^{\top}\bm{b}(\bm{x}).

Let 𝛉C,log∗\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*} denote the unique population minimizer of the πΛ\pi_{\Lambda}-stabilized logistic direct CMTP A-learning loss

ℓA,CMTPNLL​(𝜽):=𝔼⁡[∑λ∈{0,1}1πiλ​(𝜼∗)​{−Yi​giλ​(𝜼∗)​𝒃i⊤​𝜽+b⁡(giλ​(𝜼∗)​𝒃i⊤​𝜽)}],b⁡(v)=log⁡(1+ev),\ell_{A,\mathrm{CMTP}}^{\mathrm{NLL}}(\bm{\theta}):=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{\lambda\in\{0,1\}}\frac{1}{\pi_{i}^{\lambda}(\bm{\eta}^{*})}\left\{-Y_{i}\,g_{i}^{\lambda}(\bm{\eta}^{*})\,\bm{b}_{i}^{\top}\bm{\theta}+b\!\left(g_{i}^{\lambda}(\bm{\eta}^{*})\,\bm{b}_{i}^{\top}\bm{\theta}\right)\right\}\right],\qquad b(v)=\log(1+e^{v}),

i.e. the solution to the population estimating equation

ΨC,log​(𝜽,𝜼∗):=𝔼⁡[∑λ∈{0,1}giλ​(𝜼∗)πiλ​(𝜼∗)​𝒃i​{Yi−μ⁡(giλ​(𝜼∗)​𝒃i⊤​𝜽)}]=𝟎.\Psi_{C,\log}(\bm{\theta},\bm{\eta}^{*}):=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{\lambda\in\{0,1\}}\frac{g_{i}^{\lambda}(\bm{\eta}^{*})}{\pi_{i}^{\lambda}(\bm{\eta}^{*})}\,\bm{b}_{i}\left\{Y_{i}-\mu\!\left(g_{i}^{\lambda}(\bm{\eta}^{*})\,\bm{b}_{i}^{\top}\bm{\theta}\right)\right\}\right]=\bm{0}. (23)

Define the bread matrix

𝑫C,log:=𝔼⁡[∑λ∈{0,1}{giλ​(𝜼∗)}2πiλ​(𝜼∗)​μ′​(giλ​(𝜼∗)​𝒃i⊤​𝜽C,log∗)​𝒃i​𝒃i⊤],\bm{D}_{C,\log}:=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{\lambda\in\{0,1\}}\frac{\{g_{i}^{\lambda}(\bm{\eta}^{*})\}^{2}}{\pi_{i}^{\lambda}(\bm{\eta}^{*})}\,\mu^{\prime}\!\left(g_{i}^{\lambda}(\bm{\eta}^{*})\,\bm{b}_{i}^{\top}\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*}\right)\bm{b}_{i}\bm{b}_{i}^{\top}\right],

and the influence function

φC,log​(𝑶i,𝜽C,log∗,𝜼∗):=∑λ∈{0,1}giλ​(𝜼∗)πiλ​(𝜼∗)​𝒃i​{Yi−μ⁡(giλ​(𝜼∗)​𝒃i⊤​𝜽C,log∗)}.\varphi_{C,\log}(\bm{O}_{i};\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*}):=\sum_{\lambda\in\{0,1\}}\frac{g_{i}^{\lambda}(\bm{\eta}^{*})}{\pi_{i}^{\lambda}(\bm{\eta}^{*})}\,\bm{b}_{i}\left\{Y_{i}-\mu\!\left(g_{i}^{\lambda}(\bm{\eta}^{*})\,\bm{b}_{i}^{\top}\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*}\right)\right\}.

Assume conditions (C1)–(C3) for the propensity model πΛ​(a,𝐱,𝛈)\pi_{\Lambda}(a,\bm{x};\bm{\eta}), that 𝛉C,log∗\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*} lies in the interior of a compact parameter space, that 𝔼​‖𝐛⁡(𝐗)‖2<∞\mathbb{E}\|\bm{b}(\bm{X})\|^{2}<\infty, that min⁡{πi0​(𝛈∗),πi1​(𝛈∗)}≥c0>0\min\{\pi_{i}^{0}(\bm{\eta}^{*}),\pi_{i}^{1}(\bm{\eta}^{*})\}\geq c_{0}>0 almost surely for some constant c0c_{0}, and that 𝐃C,log\bm{D}_{C,\log} is nonsingular.

Let 𝛉^C,log\widehat{\bm{\theta}}_{C,\log} solve the empirical estimating equation

ΨC,log,n​(𝜽,𝜼^n):=ℙn​[ψC,log​(𝑶i,𝜽,𝜼^n)]=𝟎.\Psi_{C,\log,n}(\bm{\theta},\widehat{\bm{\eta}}_{n}):=\mathbb{P}_{n}\bigl[\psi_{C,\log}(\bm{O}_{i};\bm{\theta},\widehat{\bm{\eta}}_{n})\bigr]=\bm{0}.

Then, as n→∞n\to\infty,

n​(𝜽^C,log−𝜽C,log∗)→𝑑N⁡(𝟎,𝑫C,log−1​𝚺C,log​(𝜽C,log∗,𝜼∗)​𝑫C,log−1),\sqrt{n}\,\bigl(\widehat{\bm{\theta}}_{C,\log}-\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*}\bigr)\;\xrightarrow{d}\;N\!\Bigl(\bm{0},\;\bm{D}_{C,\log}^{-1}\,\bm{\Sigma}_{C,\log}(\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*};\bm{\eta}^{*})\,\bm{D}_{C,\log}^{-1}\Bigr),

where

𝚺C,log​(𝜽C,log∗,𝜼∗):=𝔼⁡[{φC,log​(𝑶i,𝜽C,log∗,𝜼∗)−𝑩C,log​J𝜼−1​U𝜼​(𝑶i,𝜼∗)}⊗2],\displaystyle\bm{\Sigma}_{C,\log}(\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*};\bm{\eta}^{*}):=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\Bigl\{\varphi_{C,\log}(\bm{O}_{i};\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*})-\bm{B}_{C,\log}\,J_{\bm{\eta}}^{-1}\,U_{\bm{\eta}}(\bm{O}_{i};\bm{\eta}^{*})\Bigr\}^{\otimes 2}\right],
𝑩C,log:=∂∂𝜼⊤​ΨC,log​(𝜽C,log∗,𝜼)|𝜼=𝜼∗,\displaystyle\bm{B}_{C,\log}:=\frac{\partial}{\partial\bm{\eta}^{\top}}\Psi_{C,\log}(\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*},\bm{\eta})\Bigg|_{\bm{\eta}=\bm{\eta}^{*}},

with J𝛈J_{\bm{\eta}} and U𝛈​(𝐎i,𝛈)U_{\bm{\eta}}(\bm{O}_{i};\bm{\eta}) as in condition (C1), and 𝐕⊗2=𝐕​𝐕⊤\bm{V}^{\otimes 2}=\bm{V}\bm{V}^{\top}. If, in addition, 𝛈^n\widehat{\bm{\eta}}_{n} is an efficient estimator of 𝛈∗\bm{\eta}^{*} with asymptotic variance 𝐕𝛈\bm{V}_{\bm{\eta}}, then 𝚺C,log​(𝛉C,log∗,𝛈∗)=𝚺~C,log​(𝛉C,log∗,𝛈∗)−𝐁C,log​𝐕𝛈​𝐁C,log⊤\bm{\Sigma}_{C,\log}(\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*};\bm{\eta}^{*})=\widetilde{\bm{\Sigma}}_{C,\log}(\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*};\bm{\eta}^{*})-\bm{B}_{C,\log}\,\bm{V}_{\bm{\eta}}\,\bm{B}_{C,\log}^{\top}, where 𝚺~C,log​(𝛉C,log∗,𝛈∗):=𝔼⁡[φC,log​(𝐎i,𝛉C,log∗,𝛈∗)⊗2]\widetilde{\bm{\Sigma}}_{C,\log}(\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*};\bm{\eta}^{*}):=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\varphi_{C,\log}(\bm{O}_{i};\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*})^{\otimes 2}\bigr] is the variance when πΛ\pi_{\Lambda} is known.

Proof of Theorem 4.

The proof follows the M-estimation strategy used in Theorem 3, with two structural differences: (i) the basis functions are 𝒃⁡(𝑿)\bm{b}(\bm{X}) rather than 𝒃⁡(A,𝑿)\bm{b}(A,\bm{X}), so the score does not depend on AA beyond what enters through the centered arm scores giλg_{i}^{\lambda}; and (ii) the πΛ−1\pi_{\Lambda}^{-1} stabilization factor introduces an additional layer in the propensity-derivative calculation.

Step 1: Identification and regularity. Write πλ:=πiλ​(𝜼∗)\pi^{\lambda}:=\pi_{i}^{\lambda}(\bm{\eta}^{*}), gλ:=giλ​(𝜼∗)g^{\lambda}:=g_{i}^{\lambda}(\bm{\eta}^{*}), and ηCλ​(𝜽):=gλ​𝒃i⊤​𝜽\eta_{C}^{\lambda}(\bm{\theta}):=g^{\lambda}\,\bm{b}_{i}^{\top}\bm{\theta}. Consider a generic duplicated row with (AΛ,𝑿)=(a,𝒙)(A_{\Lambda},\bm{X})=(a,\bm{x}) and write π∗:=πΛ​(𝒙,a,𝜼∗)\pi^{*}:=\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a;\bm{\eta}^{*}). Conditional on (AΛ,𝑿)=(a,𝒙)(A_{\Lambda},\bm{X})=(a,\bm{x}), the arm indicator satisfies Λ~=1\widetilde{\Lambda}=1 with probability π∗\pi^{*}, and, by consistency and Assumption 3(A′) as in Proposition 2, 𝔼[Y∣Λ~=1,AΛ=a,𝑿=𝒙]=m0(a+δ,𝒙)\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\widetilde{\Lambda}=1,A_{\Lambda}=a,\bm{X}=\bm{x}]=m_{0}(a+\delta,\bm{x}) and 𝔼[Y∣Λ~=0,AΛ=a,𝑿=𝒙]=m0(a,𝒙)\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\widetilde{\Lambda}=0,A_{\Lambda}=a,\bm{X}=\bm{x}]=m_{0}(a,\bm{x}). Hence the row-level score s⁡(𝜽):={(Λ~−π∗)/π∗}​𝒃​(𝒙)​{Y−μ⁡((Λ~−π∗)​𝒃​(𝒙)⊤​𝜽)}s(\bm{\theta}):=\{(\widetilde{\Lambda}-\pi^{*})/\pi^{*}\}\,\bm{b}(\bm{x})\{Y-\mu((\widetilde{\Lambda}-\pi^{*})\,\bm{b}(\bm{x})^{\top}\bm{\theta})\} satisfies

𝔼[s(𝜽)∣AΛ=a,𝑿=𝒙]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[s(\bm{\theta})\mid A_{\Lambda}=a,\bm{X}=\bm{x}\bigr]
={1−π∗}​𝒃​(𝒙)​[{m0​(a+δ,𝒙)−m0​(a,𝒙)}−{μ⁡((1−π∗)​𝒃​(𝒙)⊤​𝜽)−μ⁡(−π∗​𝒃​(𝒙)⊤​𝜽)}].\displaystyle=\{1-\pi^{*}\}\,\bm{b}(\bm{x})\Bigl[\bigl\{m_{0}(a+\delta,\bm{x})-m_{0}(a,\bm{x})\bigr\}-\bigl\{\mu\bigl((1-\pi^{*})\,\bm{b}(\bm{x})^{\top}\bm{\theta}\bigr)-\mu\bigl(-\pi^{*}\,\bm{b}(\bm{x})^{\top}\bm{\theta}\bigr)\bigr\}\Bigr].

Averaging over the duplicated-arm mixture law of AΛA_{\Lambda} given 𝑿=𝒙\bm{X}=\bm{x}, with conditional density fAΛ|𝑿​(a∣𝒙)=12​{gA|𝑿​(a∣𝒙)+gA|𝑿​(a+δ∣𝒙)}f_{A_{\Lambda}\mid\bm{X}}(a\mid\bm{x})=\tfrac{1}{2}\{g_{A\mid\bm{X}}(a\mid\bm{x})+g_{A\mid\bm{X}}(a+\delta\mid\bm{x})\}, and using the identity {1−πΛ​(𝒙,a)}​fAΛ|𝑿​(a∣𝒙)=12​gA|𝑿​(a∣𝒙)\{1-\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},a)\}\,f_{A_{\Lambda}\mid\bm{X}}(a\mid\bm{x})=\tfrac{1}{2}\,g_{A\mid\bm{X}}(a\mid\bm{x}), the per-subject score (which sums the two rows and thus equals twice the per-row mixture average in expectation) satisfies

ΨC,log​(𝜽,𝜼∗)=𝔼⁡[𝒃⁡(𝑿)​{τδ​(𝑿)−χ⁡(𝑿,𝜽)}],\displaystyle\Psi_{C,\log}(\bm{\theta},\bm{\eta}^{*})=\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\bm{b}(\bm{X})\,\bigl\{\tau_{\delta}(\bm{X})-\chi(\bm{X};\bm{\theta})\bigr\}\Bigr],
χ⁡(𝒙,𝜽):=𝔼⁡[μ⁡({1−πΛ​(𝒙,A)}​𝒃​(𝒙)⊤​𝜽)−μ⁡(−πΛ​(𝒙,A)​𝒃​(𝒙)⊤​𝜽)|𝑿=𝒙],\displaystyle\chi(\bm{x};\bm{\theta}):=\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\mu\bigl(\{1-\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},A)\}\,\bm{b}(\bm{x})^{\top}\bm{\theta}\bigr)-\mu\bigl(-\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{x},A)\,\bm{b}(\bm{x})^{\top}\bm{\theta}\bigr)\,\Big|\,\bm{X}=\bm{x}\Bigr],

where the inner expectation is over the natural conditional law of AA given 𝑿=𝒙\bm{X}=\bm{x} and τδ​(𝒙)=𝔼⁡[m0​(A+δ,𝒙)−m0​(A,𝒙)∣𝑿=𝒙]\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x})=\mathbb{E}[m_{0}(A+\delta,\bm{x})-m_{0}(A,\bm{x})\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}] by Proposition 2. Thus (23) defines a link-scale projection of the CMTP: if χ⁡(𝒙,𝜽0)=τδ​(𝒙)\chi(\bm{x};\bm{\theta}_{0})=\tau_{\delta}(\bm{x}) for some 𝜽0\bm{\theta}_{0} and P𝑿P_{\bm{X}}-almost every 𝒙\bm{x}, then 𝜽C,log∗=𝜽0\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*}=\bm{\theta}_{0}; this is the NLL analogue of Proposition 5 and parallels Proposition 6. This also establishes the derivations of the direct CMTP losses for the logistic case promised in Section A.3. Uniqueness follows from strict convexity of the stabilized loss, whose Hessian at any 𝜽\bm{\theta} is 𝔼⁡[∑λ{giλ}2​{πiλ}−1​μ′​(ηCλ​(𝜽))​𝒃i​𝒃i⊤]≻0\mathbb{E}[\sum_{\lambda}\{g_{i}^{\lambda}\}^{2}\{\pi_{i}^{\lambda}\}^{-1}\mu^{\prime}(\eta_{C}^{\lambda}(\bm{\theta}))\,\bm{b}_{i}\bm{b}_{i}^{\top}]\succ 0. In particular, the bread of the M-estimator at 𝜽C,log∗\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*} is

𝑫C,log=−∂∂𝜽⊤​ΨC,log​(𝜽,𝜼∗)|𝜽=𝜽C,log∗=𝔼⁡[∑λ∈{0,1}{giλ}2πiλ​μ′​(ηCλ​(𝜽C,log∗))​𝒃i​𝒃i⊤],\bm{D}_{C,\log}=-\frac{\partial}{\partial\bm{\theta}^{\top}}\Psi_{C,\log}(\bm{\theta},\bm{\eta}^{*})\bigg|_{\bm{\theta}=\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*}}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{\lambda\in\{0,1\}}\frac{\{g_{i}^{\lambda}\}^{2}}{\pi_{i}^{\lambda}}\,\mu^{\prime}\!\bigl(\eta_{C}^{\lambda}(\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*})\bigr)\,\bm{b}_{i}\bm{b}_{i}^{\top}\right],

which is nonsingular by assumption.

Step 2: Asymptotic linear representation. Since 𝜽^C,log\widehat{\bm{\theta}}_{C,\log} solves ΨC,log,n​(𝜽^C,log,𝜼^n)=𝟎\Psi_{C,\log,n}(\widehat{\bm{\theta}}_{C,\log},\widehat{\bm{\eta}}_{n})=\bm{0}, a first-order Taylor expansion around (𝜽C,log∗,𝜼∗)(\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*}) gives

𝟎\displaystyle\bm{0} =ΨC,log,n​(𝜽C,log∗,𝜼∗)+Ψ˙C,log,n,𝜽​(𝜽C,log∗,𝜼∗)​(𝜽^C,log−𝜽C,log∗)\displaystyle=\Psi_{C,\log,n}(\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*})+\dot{\Psi}_{C,\log,n,\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*})\bigl(\widehat{\bm{\theta}}_{C,\log}-\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*}\bigr)
+Ψ˙C,log,n,𝜼​(𝜽C,log∗,𝜼∗)​(𝜼^n−𝜼∗)+rn,\displaystyle\qquad+\dot{\Psi}_{C,\log,n,\bm{\eta}}(\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*})\bigl(\widehat{\bm{\eta}}_{n}-\bm{\eta}^{*}\bigr)+r_{n}, (24)

where ∥rn∥=op(n−1/2)\|r_{n}\|=o_{p}(n^{-1/2}) by the twice-continuous differentiability of μ\mu, the compactness of the parameter space, and the Donsker property of the relevant function classes (see below). Rearranging and multiplying by n\sqrt{n},

n​(𝜽^C,log−𝜽C,log∗)\displaystyle\sqrt{n}\,\bigl(\widehat{\bm{\theta}}_{C,\log}-\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*}\bigr)
=−Ψ˙C,log,n,𝜽​(𝜽C,log∗,𝜼∗)−1​{n​ΨC,log,n​(𝜽C,log∗,𝜼∗)+Ψ˙C,log,n,𝜼​(𝜽C,log∗,𝜼∗)​n​(𝜼^n−𝜼∗)}+op​(1).\displaystyle=-\dot{\Psi}_{C,\log,n,\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*})^{-1}\Bigl\{\sqrt{n}\,\Psi_{C,\log,n}(\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*})+\dot{\Psi}_{C,\log,n,\bm{\eta}}(\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*})\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\bm{\eta}}_{n}-\bm{\eta}^{*})\Bigr\}+o_{p}(1). (25)

Step 3: Limits of the derivative terms. For the 𝜽\bm{\theta}-derivative,

Ψ˙C,log,n,𝜽​(𝜽C,log∗,𝜼∗)=−ℙn​[∑λ∈{0,1}{giλ}2πiλ​μ′​(ηCλ​(𝜽C,log∗))​𝒃i​𝒃i⊤]→𝑝−𝑫C,log.\dot{\Psi}_{C,\log,n,\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*})=-\mathbb{P}_{n}\!\left[\sum_{\lambda\in\{0,1\}}\frac{\{g_{i}^{\lambda}\}^{2}}{\pi_{i}^{\lambda}}\mu^{\prime}\!\bigl(\eta_{C}^{\lambda}(\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*})\bigr)\bm{b}_{i}\bm{b}_{i}^{\top}\right]\;\xrightarrow{p}\;-\bm{D}_{C,\log}.

This convergence follows from the law of large numbers, using 𝔼⁡[∑λ𝒃i​𝒃i⊤​{giλ}2/πiλ​μ′​(ηCλ)]<∞\mathbb{E}[\sum_{\lambda}\bm{b}_{i}\bm{b}_{i}^{\top}\{g_{i}^{\lambda}\}^{2}/\pi_{i}^{\lambda}\,\mu^{\prime}(\eta_{C}^{\lambda})]<\infty (implied by πiλ≥c0>0\pi_{i}^{\lambda}\geq c_{0}>0, compactness of the parameter space, and μ′≤1/4\mu^{\prime}\leq 1/4). Since 𝑫C,log\bm{D}_{C,\log} is nonsingular, Ψ˙C,log,n,𝜽−1\dot{\Psi}_{C,\log,n,\bm{\theta}}^{-1} is well-defined with probability approaching 1.

For the 𝜼\bm{\eta}-derivative, let π˙iλ:=∂πΛ​(𝒁iλ,𝜼)/∂𝜼|𝜼=𝜼∗\dot{\pi}_{i}^{\lambda}:=\partial\pi_{\Lambda}(\bm{Z}_{i}^{\lambda};\bm{\eta})/\partial\bm{\eta}\big|_{\bm{\eta}=\bm{\eta}^{*}}. Using ∂giλ/∂𝜼=−π˙iλ\partial g_{i}^{\lambda}/\partial\bm{\eta}=-\dot{\pi}_{i}^{\lambda} and ∂{giλ/πiλ}/∂𝜼=−λπ˙iλ/(πiλ)2\partial\{g_{i}^{\lambda}/\pi_{i}^{\lambda}\}/\partial\bm{\eta}=-\lambda\,\dot{\pi}_{i}^{\lambda}/(\pi_{i}^{\lambda})^{2} (note giλ/πiλ=λ/πiλ−1g_{i}^{\lambda}/\pi_{i}^{\lambda}=\lambda/\pi_{i}^{\lambda}-1), the chain rule gives, for each component ℓ\ell of 𝜼\bm{\eta},

∂∂𝜼ℓ​{giλπiλ​𝒃i​(Yi−μ⁡(ηCλ​(𝜽C,log∗)))}\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial\bm{\eta}_{\ell}}\left\{\frac{g_{i}^{\lambda}}{\pi_{i}^{\lambda}}\,\bm{b}_{i}\bigl(Y_{i}-\mu(\eta_{C}^{\lambda}(\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*}))\bigr)\right\}
=−λ​π˙i,ℓλ(πiλ)2​𝒃i​(Yi−μ⁡(ηCλ​(𝜽C,log∗)))+giλπiλ​μ′​(ηCλ​(𝜽C,log∗))​π˙i,ℓλ​𝒃i​𝒃i⊤​𝜽C,log∗,\displaystyle=-\frac{\lambda\,\dot{\pi}_{i,\ell}^{\lambda}}{(\pi_{i}^{\lambda})^{2}}\,\bm{b}_{i}\bigl(Y_{i}-\mu(\eta_{C}^{\lambda}(\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*}))\bigr)+\frac{g_{i}^{\lambda}}{\pi_{i}^{\lambda}}\,\mu^{\prime}\!\bigl(\eta_{C}^{\lambda}(\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*})\bigr)\,\dot{\pi}_{i,\ell}^{\lambda}\;\bm{b}_{i}\,\bm{b}_{i}^{\top}\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*},

and the first term vanishes for λ=0\lambda=0 since gi0/πi0≡−1g_{i}^{0}/\pi_{i}^{0}\equiv-1. By the Donsker property of {πΛ​(⋅,𝜼):𝜼∈ℋ∗}\{\pi_{\Lambda}(\cdot;\bm{\eta}):\bm{\eta}\in\mathcal{H}^{*}\} and its derivative (Lipschitz in 𝜼\bm{\eta} by (C3), hence Donsker by Example 19.7 of van der Vaart (1998)), together with the smoothness of μ\mu and the moment conditions, the empirical derivative converges in probability to its population counterpart:

Ψ˙C,log,n,𝜼​(𝜽C,log∗,𝜼∗)→𝑝𝑩C,log:=∂∂𝜼⊤​ΨC,log​(𝜽C,log∗,𝜼)|𝜼=𝜼∗.\dot{\Psi}_{C,\log,n,\bm{\eta}}(\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*})\;\xrightarrow{p}\;\bm{B}_{C,\log}:=\frac{\partial}{\partial\bm{\eta}^{\top}}\Psi_{C,\log}(\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*},\bm{\eta})\Big|_{\bm{\eta}=\bm{\eta}^{*}}.

Step 4: Empirical process term. Since P⁡[φC,log​(𝑶i,𝜽C,log∗,𝜼∗)]=𝟎P[\varphi_{C,\log}(\bm{O}_{i};\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*})]=\bm{0} by definition of 𝜽C,log∗\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*}, we have

n​ΨC,log,n​(𝜽C,log∗,𝜼∗)=𝔾n​[φC,log​(𝑶i,𝜽C,log∗,𝜼∗)]=Op​(1).\sqrt{n}\,\Psi_{C,\log,n}(\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*})=\mathbb{G}_{n}\bigl[\varphi_{C,\log}(\bm{O}_{i};\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*})\bigr]=O_{p}(1).

The class {φC,log(⋅;𝜽,𝜼):𝜽∈𝒯,𝜼∈ℋ∗}\{\varphi_{C,\log}(\cdot;\bm{\theta},\bm{\eta}):\bm{\theta}\in\mathcal{T},\bm{\eta}\in\mathcal{H}^{*}\} is Donsker: it is a product of π−1\pi^{-1}-bounded, Lipschitz functions of 𝜼\bm{\eta} (by (C3) and πiλ≥c0\pi_{i}^{\lambda}\geq c_{0}), the bounded function Y−μ⁡(g​𝒃⊤​𝜽)Y-\mu(g\,\bm{b}^{\top}\bm{\theta}) (bounded because μ∈(0,1)\mu\in(0,1)), and the fixed 𝒃⁡(𝑿)\bm{b}(\bm{X}); note that 𝔾n\mathbb{G}_{n} acts on the per-subject summed score φC,log​(𝑶i,⋅)\varphi_{C,\log}(\bm{O}_{i};\cdot), which is i.i.d. across subjects and correctly accounts for the fact that a subject’s two duplicated rows share YiY_{i}. By the central limit theorem for Donsker classes,

𝔾n​[φC,log​(𝑶i,𝜽C,log∗,𝜼∗)]→𝑑N⁡(𝟎,𝚺~C,log​(𝜽C,log∗,𝜼∗)),\mathbb{G}_{n}\bigl[\varphi_{C,\log}(\bm{O}_{i};\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*})\bigr]\;\xrightarrow{d}\;N\!\bigl(\bm{0},\,\widetilde{\bm{\Sigma}}_{C,\log}(\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*};\bm{\eta}^{*})\bigr),

n​(𝜼^n−𝜼∗)=−J𝜼−1​𝔾n​[U𝜼​(𝑶i,𝜼∗)]+op​(1).\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\bm{\eta}}_{n}-\bm{\eta}^{*})=-\,J_{\bm{\eta}}^{-1}\mathbb{G}_{n}\bigl[U_{\bm{\eta}}(\bm{O}_{i};\bm{\eta}^{*})\bigr]+o_{p}(1).

with

𝚺C,log=𝔼⁡[{φC,log​(𝑶i,𝜽C,log∗,𝜼∗)−𝑩C,log​J𝜼−1​U𝜼​(𝑶i,𝜼∗)}⊗2].\bm{\Sigma}_{C,\log}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\Bigl\{\varphi_{C,\log}(\bm{O}_{i};\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*},\bm{\eta}^{*})-\bm{B}_{C,\log}\,J_{\bm{\eta}}^{-1}U_{\bm{\eta}}(\bm{O}_{i};\bm{\eta}^{*})\Bigr\}^{\otimes 2}\right].

If 𝜼^n\widehat{\bm{\eta}}_{n} is efficient for 𝜼∗\bm{\eta}^{*} with asymptotic variance 𝑽𝜼\bm{V}_{\bm{\eta}}, and is jointly asymptotically normal with 𝔾n​φC,log\mathbb{G}_{n}\varphi_{C,\log}, then by the variance-reduction argument of Pierce (1982), the covariance matrix reduces to

𝚺C,log​(𝜽C,log∗,𝜼∗)=𝚺~C,log​(𝜽C,log∗,𝜼∗)−𝑩C,log​𝑽𝜼​𝑩C,log⊤,\bm{\Sigma}_{C,\log}(\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*};\bm{\eta}^{*})=\widetilde{\bm{\Sigma}}_{C,\log}(\bm{\theta}_{C,\log}^{*};\bm{\eta}^{*})-\bm{B}_{C,\log}\,\bm{V}_{\bm{\eta}}\,\bm{B}_{C,\log}^{\top},
